item.title: DMCH patients face risks from stagnant water and poor sanitation
item.description:
Amid the dengue outbreak, patients from different parts of the country are coming to Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH) for treatment. However, stagnant water, dirt, waste and unhygienic conditions in various parts of the hospital are increasing the risk of mosquito breeding and the spread of disease-causing germs.
In one building, sewage was also seen leaking through a hole in a toilet pipe on the third floor and spreading to the surrounding area.
During an on-site visit, stagnant water was found in several open drains and holes after entering the hospital through its outpatient department. Water had also accumulated in discarded coconut shells and tea cups, with signs indicating that it had been there for a long time.
Water dripping from air-conditioning (AC) units was also accumulating in different places. Cigarette butts, tissue paper and other waste were floating in the water. While the accumulated water was clear in some places, it was dirty in others.
Mosquitoes were visible in the stagnant water, while numerous patients waited nearby for their turn to receive treatment.
According to experts, Aedes mosquito larvae can develop in stagnant water within just three days under favourable conditions. Therefore, removing stagnant water and maintaining cleanliness in hospitals and other public places are crucial during a dengue outbreak.
Entomologist Professor Kabirul Bashar said: “The risk is even greater when Aedes mosquitoes breed in a hospital, as many patients receive treatment there. This also increases the risk of disease transmission. For this reason, the premises of every hospital should be inspected at least once a week to check whether water has accumulated in any place or container. These areas must be cleaned regularly. Under no circumstances should Aedes mosquitoes be allowed to breed around hospitals. Keeping hospital premises clean is essential.”
Photo: Dhaka Tribune
He added that Aedes mosquitoes can breed in both clear and dirty water, provided it remains stagnant. Their larvae do not develop in flowing water.
Bashar said Aedes mosquito larvae could develop in stagnant water within three days, while an egg takes around seven days to develop into an adult mosquito. Aedes mosquitoes lay their eggs on the sides of containers near the waterline, whereas Culex mosquitoes lay their eggs on the water’s surface.
Therefore, water must not be allowed to accumulate anywhere on hospital premises, and cleanliness must be maintained.
Water has also accumulated beside the hospital’s paediatric ward, spreading a foul stench. Mosquitoes have also been spotted in the area.
Mochammat Asiya brought her son, who has been diagnosed with dengue, to Dhaka Medical College Hospital for treatment.
Asiya said: “We come here for treatment hoping to recover. However, if water accumulates in different places and the environment remains unclean, there is a risk of becoming even sicker instead of recovering. Someone may come here for treatment for another illness and contract dengue. How can patients recover if conditions inside the hospital are like this? These issues should be brought to the attention of the hospital authorities.”
During a visit to a section of the hospital’s third floor, sewage was seen leaking through a hole in a large pipe in a washroom on the left. The leakage was spreading a foul smell throughout the surrounding area. The waste was also being carried around on people’s feet as they walked through the affected area.
Mohammad Arif is staying at the hospital with his wife, who has been admitted for treatment. He said sewage had been leaking from the pipe for the past two days, leaving them with no choice but to walk through the waste.
“I informed the cleaning staff about the problem on the very first day. However, no action has been taken yet. It is obvious how many types of germs could spread from here and how many people could fall ill. We came to the hospital to recover, yet we have to stay here amid germs and foul smells,” he said.
Pointing to another section of the hospital, Arif said dirty water had also been accumulating there for a long time. He stressed that keeping the hospital clean was essential, as patients from different parts of the country come to the facility for treatment.
In addition, water was found accumulating on the left side of the hospital after exiting the indoor department, with mosquitoes visible on its surface.
Dhaka Medical College Hospital Director Brigadier General Md Asaduzzaman said the number of patients far exceeded the hospital’s capacity. The presence of patients’ relatives also made it difficult to maintain cleanliness amid the pressure caused by the large number of people.
“However, we are continuing our cleaning activities. I have also joined recently. We are continuing our efforts as far as possible,” he said.
Regarding the sewage leaking through the hole in the toilet pipe, the director said the problem would be resolved soon. He added that work was underway to identify and address problems in various parts of the hospital.

item.title: Journalist’s murder raises questions over ignored warnings
item.description:
Journalist Lutfuzzaman Fakir Alif had warned police that his life was in danger and survived an earlier attack by armed assailants.
On Thursday night, he was shot dead outside a tea stall in Netrokona’s Durgapur in what police now believe was a premeditated killing, possibly linked to his reporting on local trafficking and smuggling networks.
The killing has raised questions about whether enough was done to protect the journalist, who had publicly spoken of threats against his life and previously filed a case after being attacked with sharp weapons.
On Saturday, Durgapur Police Station Officer-in-Charge Khandaker Shaker Ahmed Khan told Dhaka Tribune that investigators suspected an organised gang was behind the murder.
He said Alif’s reporting on trafficking, smuggling and other criminal activities could have been a motive, although police had yet to establish who ordered or carried out the killing.
The OC said several police units, including the Detective Branch (DB), Criminal Investigation Department (CID) and District Special Branch (DSB), were working to identify and arrest those responsible.
Alif, the Netrokona correspondent of private IP television channel Rupashi Bangla, also operated a Facebook page called “Detective Article”, where he published reports and videos about alleged irregularities and crimes.
Police said his work had created enemies and that he had previously been warned about possible threats.
Nearly a year before his death, Alif had publicly expressed fears that he could be attacked.
A video of him speaking at a meeting with police has resurfaced following his murder.
In the footage, Alif claimed to have received information that people threatening him were waiting on a road with firearms, including a 9mm pistol loaded with five bullets.
He said he had informed police about the threat but alleged that no attempt had been made to arrest those responsible.
Alif warned that if the suspects remained free, he might have to leave Bangladesh to protect himself.
He also spoke of the possibility of being driven into a confrontation with those threatening him.
Responding to questions about the earlier warnings, OC Shaker Ahmed Khan said police had advised Alif to inform them whenever he visited the area so that security could be arranged.
The officer acknowledged that Alif had several enemies and that police had warned him about the risks.
The fatal shooting was not the first violent attack on Alif.
On November 10 last year, assailants attacked him with sharp weapons near Teribazar ghat on the Someshwari River in Durgapur.
He sustained injuries in the attack.
When a colleague accompanying him attempted to intervene, the attackers allegedly brandished weapons and chased him away.
Alif subsequently filed a case, and police arrested two named suspects.
Both suspects were later released on bail.
Police have not established whether the earlier attack and Thursday’s killing were connected.
According to police and eyewitnesses, Alif was at a tea stall in the Telonzia area of Durgapur on Thursday evening, a short distance from his second wife’s family home.
Around 8pm, he finished drinking tea and left for Birishiri Utrail Bazar.
However, after realising he had left his mobile phone behind, he returned to the stall within approximately three minutes.
As he was leaving with his phone, two young men approached the stall and asked the shopkeeper for cigarettes.
The men then opened fire on Alif, shooting him repeatedly before fleeing.
Residents rushed to the scene after hearing the gunshots.
Alif was taken to the Upazila Health Complex, where a doctor declared him dead.
Police recovered pistol cartridge casings and an unexploded bullet from the scene.
Netrokona Superintendent of Police Md Tariqul Islam, who visited the location, also said preliminary findings suggested the killing had been planned.
A post-mortem examination conducted at Netrokona Modern Sadar Hospital on Friday found six bullet wounds on Alif’s body.
Dr Shraddhyananda Nath, who conducted the examination, said three wounds were in the chest.
Two bullets passed through his body, while another remained lodged in his back.
One bullet entered through the right side of his forehead and exited through the back of his head.
Two other bullets grazed the skin on his head and near his right shoulder.
Based on the injuries, the physician initially believed Alif had been shot from the front with a pistol.
The findings indicate that the journalist was struck by multiple shots at close range, although the precise distance has not been established.
Alif’s wife, Anandita Sangma, said she was feeding their children when she heard the gunfire.
At first, she thought someone was setting off firecrackers.
Moments later, people began shouting that her husband had been killed.
Anandita said she had never imagined that Alif would be shot dead in such a manner.
She demanded that police identify the killers and ensure exemplary punishment for those who had left her two children without their father.
Alif’s elder brother, Shahid Islam Fakir, said the journalist had made many enemies through his reporting.
He also demanded justice for the killing.
Alif was originally from Sunoi village in Kalmakanda upazila of Netrokona but had been living at his second wife’s family home in Telonzia, Durgapur.
Following the post-mortem examination, his body was buried in the family graveyard in Sunoi village.
Anandita filed a murder case with Durgapur Police Station on Friday night, accusing seven to eight unidentified individuals.
Police said they were conducting operations to identify the attackers and determine whether Alif’s reporting on criminal activities had prompted the killing.
OC Shaker Ahmed Khan said investigators were working to establish the identities of the perpetrators and bring them to justice.
He said police suspected an organised group was involved and that the killing had been planned.
However, no arrests had been reported as of Saturday afternoon.
The investigation will also have to establish whether the threats Alif reported to police, the earlier armed attack and his eventual murder were linked.

item.title: PM’s visit brings a quick makeover to Shaheed Suhrawardy Hospital
item.description:
The poor condition of Bangladesh’s public hospitals has long been a source of public concern. Yet, the announcement of a visit by the prime minister can prompt a swift transformation, with cleaning and renovation work carried out within days. Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College and Hospital in Dhaka offered a glimpse of this contrast on Thursday, ahead of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit.
On Saturday, the prime minister visited the hospital and 12 other medical facilities, including the Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute. During the visits, he spoke with officials and patients and inspected cleanliness, service quality and overall management.
At the children’s hospital, he reportedly found Associate Professor Dr Rafiqul Islam smoking in his office, which was also found to be unclean. The prime minister immediately instructed the hospital chairman to take action against the physician. Dr Rafiqul Islam was subsequently placed under temporary suspension.
At Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College and Hospital, cleaning and renovation work had been underway since Thursday. Workers were washing floors, plastering and painting walls, laying tiles and repairing toilets in the outpatient and emergency departments.
The hospital’s outpatient department treats around 3,500 patients daily, while the emergency department handles approximately 1,500. The patient load far exceeds the facility’s capacity, leaving doctors, interns and nurses struggling to maintain services.
The flurry of activity, however, comes against a backdrop of chronic overcrowding, staff shortages and inadequate facilities that continue to undermine patient care.
Hospital authorities said nearly 5,000 dengue patients received treatment between July and September, with seven deaths recorded during the period. Dental services remain limited despite the presence of a dental unit, while a shortage of anaesthesiologists has disrupted services in neurosurgery, orthopaedics, paediatric surgery and ear, nose and throat (ENT) care.
The lack of adequate sanitation facilities is particularly striking. The outpatient department has 10 toilets for around 3,500 patients a day, while the emergency department has five for approximately 1,500 patients. Some toilets are unusable and remain locked, while a foul stench hangs around the facilities.
Repairs to several toilets were also underway ahead of the prime minister’s visit.
Asked about the inspection, hospital Director Dr Mirza Golam Sarwar told Dhaka Tribune on Saturday afternoon that the prime minister had inspected the outpatient and emergency departments, checked on admitted patients and visited the kitchen, toilets and other areas. He also spoke with patients.
Suhrawardy Hospital gets facelift centering PM’s visit, on Thursday, October 15, 2026. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
When asked about the ongoing cleaning and renovation work, limited dental services and the shortage of anaesthesiologists, the director said preparations for the inspection had placed the hospital administration under considerable pressure.
“We have been losing sleep over the hospital inspection. I am exhausted and cannot comment on anything at the moment,” he said.
During a visit on Thursday, workers were seen cleaning floors, walls and ward fans, repairing toilets and repainting sections of the outpatient and emergency departments. Faulty electrical equipment was also being replaced.
Emergency Department In-charge Dr Md Bin Mizan told Dhaka Tribune that cleaning was a regular activity and was not being carried out solely because of the prime minister’s visit.
He said the outpatient and emergency departments faced an exceptionally heavy patient load and therefore required particular attention.
Inside the emergency department, doctors continued treating patients as workers cleaned beds and wiped down fans. Asked whether the work was causing inconvenience to patients, several interns acknowledged that cleaning was underway but appeared resigned to the situation.
Hospital authorities said the facility provided services to 143,977 patients between January and September this year, including 44,159 patients in the emergency department.
The outpatient department treats around 3,500 patients daily, while the emergency department handles approximately 1,500. Typically, six to eight medical officers, along with interns, work in the emergency department.
Dr Bin Mizan said staff struggled to cope with the enormous patient load.
Although the hospital has a dental unit, shortages of modern equipment, space and personnel prevent it from providing comprehensive services.
Limited ticket availability, long queues and logistical constraints further restrict access to treatment.
Dental physician Syed Faridur Rahman told Dhaka Tribune that the unit continued to provide care despite shortages of space and equipment. He said the hospital lacked adequate modern dental chairs, X-ray facilities and other surgical equipment.
While routine procedures such as scaling, fillings and tooth extractions were available, patients often had to wait for extended periods for root canal treatment, complex orthodontic procedures and major oral and maxillofacial surgeries. The hospital also does not offer dental crown fitting.
Meanwhile, a shortage of anaesthesiologists has affected services in neurosurgery, orthopaedics, paediatric surgery and ENT.
Dr Bin Mizan said five physician posts remained vacant, making it difficult to provide daily services to patients requiring treatment in these specialised departments.
Hospital authorities said nearly 5,000 dengue patients received treatment between July and September, with seven deaths recorded during the three-month period.
Dr Bin Mizan said the heavy influx of dengue patients made maintaining cleanliness particularly important. Hospital staff tried to keep the premises clean around the clock, but the workload remained overwhelming.
He added that some patients spat betel juice on the floors and left toilets dirty, making it more difficult for cleaners to maintain hygiene.
Hospital cleaners said around 3,500 men and women visited the outpatient department daily, which has 10 toilets. However, some remain locked because they are damaged, reducing the number available for use.
As a result, the department has roughly one toilet for every 350 daily patients. The emergency department has five toilets for approximately 1,500 patients a day.
Salma Begum, a cleaner responsible for maintaining the toilets, told Dhaka Tribune on Thursday that she and her colleagues tried to keep the facilities clean but often struggled to cope with the waste left behind.
She said patients frequently discarded water bottles, tissues, sanitary pads, clothes and other rubbish in the toilets, causing some facilities to become clogged and unusable.
Several toilets were being repaired, she added.

item.title: Ishraque: Police inaction drove me to armed anti-drug raid
item.description:
State Minister for Liberation War Affairs Ishraque Hossain took a firearm and personally led an anti-drug operation in Dhaka on Saturday, saying police had failed to take effective action despite 30–40 meetings with him over drug trafficking in his constituency.
The unusual intervention near Dayaganj Ghuntighar railway crossing in Gendaria has sparked controversy after a video showed the state minister holding a pistol, armed bodyguards chasing suspected drug dealers and one security guard kicking a detained man.
The footage, posted on Ishraque’s Facebook page before being removed, also captured someone threatening to shoot, although the speaker’s identity could not be established.
The operation took place between 3pm and 3:30pm near Gendaria railway station, according to Pavel Shikdar, former convener of Dhaka Metropolitan South Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal.
In the video, Ishraque is seen stepping out of his vehicle with a firearm and shouting, “Catch them, catch them, catch them!”
Several men are subsequently detained. One is heard pleading, “Sir, I haven’t done anything! I am a poor man, sir.”
The detained individuals were later handed over to police.
Speaking to media, Ishraque said residents of his Dhaka-6 constituency had repeatedly complained about drug trafficking in the area.
He claimed police had failed to respond effectively despite numerous discussions.
“I have held at least 30 to 40 meetings with them,” he said, adding that officers frequently cited shortages of personnel and vehicles.
The state minister said he had therefore decided to intervene personally.
He claimed drug dealers sometimes opened fire during operations and that several police officers had previously suffered gunshot injuries.
Explaining why he carried a pistol, Ishraque said the weapon was legally licensed and intended for his protection.
“I did not fire any shots, nor did I use the weapon to threaten anyone,” he said.
However, the video shows him holding the firearm in the presence of civilians, including children.
Gendaria Police Station Officer-in-Charge Moniruzzaman disputed the suggestion that police had failed to act.
He said a major anti-drug operation involving around 300 police personnel, including members of the Detective Branch and Special Response Battalion, had been conducted on October 11.
The OC said police maintained regular communication with Ishraque and informed him about their operations and results.
The incident has also raised questions about the state minister’s use of a firearm.
Under the Home Ministry’s 2025 firearms policy, licensed weapons may be carried for self-defence but must not be displayed in a manner that causes fear or annoyance to others.
Ishraque said he obtained his firearm after the shooting of Sharif Osman Hadi in December 2025.
The video also shows armed security personnel accompanying Ishraque, with one bodyguard kicking a suspect.

item.title: What does the firearms policy say about Ishraque carrying a pistol during a raid
item.description:
State Minister for Liberation War Affairs and Dhaka-6 MP Ishraque Hossain led an anti-drug operation in the capital’s Gendaria area while carrying a firearm, raising questions about what a firearms license legally allows its holder to do.
The state minister raided a slum beside the railway line in Ward 45 under Gendaria police station, detaining 6 people on suspicion of drug dealing.
He posted a video of the operation on his verified Facebook page with the caption “Ishraque's Action.”
In the footage, he steps out of a car with a pistol in one hand and a microphone in the other before chasing several people. Men accompanying him catch some of them, while others run away.
“Drug dealers will not be spared, whichever party they belong to,” he said during the operation. He added that anyone from his own party found to be involved in the trade would face a heavier punishment.
He also told locals that he had been gathering information through intelligence sources for 6 months and that the campaign, which began in his constituency, would continue across the country.
The minister assured the detainees that no one would harm them.
“You will go to the police station, and the police will take action,” he said.
“This country will be run by law.”
Gendaria police station Officer-in-Charge Moniruzzaman Monir said the minister detained 6 people and called the police station.
Police then went to the spot and took them into custody.
“A white powder-like substance was found on the detainees,” the officer-in-charge said. He added that laboratory tests would determine whether it was heroin.
Bangladesh's firearms laws are governed by the Arms Act, 1878, and the Arms Rules, 1924.
The Home Ministry's Firearms License Issuance, Renewal and Use Policy, 2025, issued on July 10, 2025, further regulates licensing and use. It replaced the 2016 policy and its amendment.
Section 25 of the policy sets out conditions governing the carrying and use of licensed firearms. Its clauses include the following:
Section 25 regulates how a licensed firearm may be carried and displayed but does not specifically mention raids, searches or arrests.
Drug raids and arrests are conducted by police and other law enforcement agencies under Bangladesh's narcotics and criminal procedure laws.
The video has prompted several questions, including whether the pistol is privately licensed in the minister's name or issued through another arrangement, which would determine the applicable rules. Questions have also arisen over whether carrying a drawn weapon while chasing people in a crowded settlement is consistent with clauses (Ka) and (Kha).
Other questions concern the legal authority of a minister or lawmaker to lead such an operation, whether those accompanying him were authorized to detain people, whether police were informed beforehand or called after the detentions, and who searched the detainees and seized the substance before police arrived.
Commenting on State Minister Ishraque's participation in the anti-drug operation and his public use of a firearm, former Inspector General of Police (IGP) Muhammad Nurul Huda told Dhaka Tribune on Saturday night that the state minister could have chosen not to go, but there was no harm in his going either.
He said licensed firearms were issued precisely to deter enemies and protect oneself. The state minister perhaps felt that carrying a weapon was necessary and used it; according to the former IGP, there had been no violation of the law.
The former IGP said deputy commissioners, officers-in-charge (OCs) and assistant commissioners (ACs) were responsible for the area and should have taken charge of the operation.

item.title: One year after airport cargo village fire, safety measures strengthened
item.description:
One year after a devastating fire broke out at the cargo village of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka, authorities have strengthened fire prevention measures, increased patrols, including on holidays, and trained nearly 2,000 personnel to improve emergency preparedness.
The fire broke out on October 18, 2025, destroying goods worth thousands of crores of taka and important documents. It drew widespread attention at home and abroad.
Firefighters, along with personnel from the army, navy, air force and Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB), worked to bring the blaze under control. Although the fire was brought under initial control at around 9pm that day, firefighting operations continued until 4:55pm on October 19, taking nearly 27 hours to complete.
The incident prompted airport authorities to form an investigation committee, which made 14 recommendations to strengthen fire safety across the airport, including the cargo area. Authorities subsequently began implementing the recommendations.
The measures included installing temporary fire hydrant points in the old import cargo area, improving fire safety at the old import and export cargo facilities, installing emergency signage at the general aviation hangar complex, and repairing non-functional hydrants at Shah Amanat International Airport in Chittagong.
Other recommendations called for installing pumps, hydrants, sprinklers and fire detection systems at the general aviation hangar complex, placing fire hose boxes at four locations, establishing a permanent fire station and improving facilities for emergency response vehicles. The recommendations also covered modernizing the existing agreement with the air force and expediting the central fuel shed project.
Mehboob Khan, member (planning and operations) of the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB), said that meetings were held with all relevant agencies following last year's fire. “Almost all the recommendations are now in the process of being implemented,” he said.
He added that airlines and courier companies were responsible for safety and security within the cargo area, as CAAB had leased the premises to them. They would have to bear responsibility for accidents if they failed to address their own shortcomings, he said.
CAAB spokesperson Kawsar Mahmud said two Fire Service and Civil Defence units had been established at the airport to strengthen fire safety and ensure a rapid response to emergencies. Adequate fire hydrant points had also been installed at key locations.
Regular fire drills and emergency rescue exercises are being conducted at different offices every month to raise awareness and improve preparedness, he said.
More than 1,900 people working in the terminal building area have received training on fire safety, the use of firefighting equipment and emergency procedures.
Regular monitoring and patrols are also being conducted throughout the airport, including on public holidays and weekly days off, to identify potential risks and ensure readiness for swift action in emergencies, Kawsar added.

item.title: Kaaruj marks 7th anniversary with new home decor collection launch
item.description:
Kaaruj Bangladesh celebrated its seventh anniversary on Saturday with a gathering and the launch of seven new home décor product categories at its recently opened Centre Point outlet in Uttara.
The event brought together loyal customers, home décor enthusiasts, vloggers and members of the Kaaruj team. The new collection includes bedcovers, candles, doormats, plants, braided products, planters and laundry baskets, expanding the brand’s range of decorative and functional home products.
The celebration featured conversations, interactive games, a photo booth and home decorating tips shared by lifestyle vloggers. Guests explored the new collection, enjoyed refreshments and received gift bags. Kaaruj also offered an exclusive 10% discount on purchases made during the event.
Speaking on the occasion, Nuzhat Bari, proprietor of Kaaruj Bangladesh, said customers had played an important role in the brand’s seven-year journey.
“Our customers have been an important part of these seven years. We wanted to celebrate this milestone with the people who have supported us throughout the journey. Introducing our new collection on this occasion makes it even more special,” she said.
Kaaruj Bangladesh launches seven new home décor product categories during its seventh anniversary celebration at its Centre Point outlet in Uttara on Saturday, October 17, 2026. Photo: Courtesy
A home décor vlogger said it was encouraging to see a Bangladeshi brand experiment with different designs and offer more choices for home decoration. The new collection, the vlogger added, brought several interesting additions.
One of the customers attending the event said they had followed Kaaruj for years and were pleased to see the collection expand. Being part of the anniversary celebration made the experience even more enjoyable, the customer added.
The name Kaaruj draws inspiration from the Bengali expressions Karu Shilpo and Karu Karjo, reflecting the brand’s connection to art and craftsmanship.
Through collaborations with local artisans and the use of materials such as jute, wood and cotton, Kaaruj offers home décor accessories that combine traditional influences with contemporary design.
The anniversary event brought together the brand’s customers and creative community while marking the addition of seven new product categories to its collection.

item.title: 10 killed: Cox’s Bazar resort operated without fire safety, environmental clearance
item.description:
At least 10 people were killed and six others injured after a fire broke out at Tuptup Resort and Restaurant in Inani, Cox’s Bazar on Saturday morning.
The resort was built without clearance from the Fire Service and Civil Defence and did not have an environmental clearance certificate, officials said.
Syed Mohammad Morshed Hossain, deputy assistant director of the Cox’s Bazar Fire Service, said the authorities had warned the resort in June about fire safety violations, but the management took no action.
“Wooden structures can catch fire quickly and flames can spread rapidly in strong coastal winds. Such establishments must have portable fire extinguishers, fire alarms, hose pipes and a fire safety plan. But the resort had none of these. It also had no fire licence,” he said.
The resort had been built only seven or eight months ago, Morshed said, adding that there was also a dispute over ownership of the property. Food was prepared on the ground floor of the resort, he added.
Khandaker Mahmud Pasha, deputy director of the Department of Environment’s Cox’s Bazar district office, said the resort had not received environmental clearance.
“No environmental clearance was issued to any establishment named Tuptup Resort and Restaurant in the Patuartek area of Inani. The establishment may not even have applied for clearance,” he said.
Panna Akter, Ukhia Upazila Nirbahi Officer, said 10 bodies had been recovered and six people were injured. A total of 18 tourists were staying at the resort when the fire broke out, she said.
Six members of the same family were among those killed. They were Faria Kabir, 33, wife of Nur Alam, a senior marketing officer of Drug International working in Chuadanga; their five-year-old son Faizan Noor; his wife’s brother Nasir Uddin, 25; and her three sisters, Israt Jahan Maliha, 30, Laila Jahan Nabila, 27, and Milita Mehejabin Alvi, 23.
The identities of the other victims have yet to be confirmed.
The six injured were Mugda Medical College Hospital physician Shihab Uddin, 31; his wife Nafisa Newaz Khan, 29; Mannan, 34; Meherunnesa, 30; Masud, 30; and Samida, 32.
“We initially believe that six of the deceased may be members of the same family. However, this will be confirmed through DNA testing,” said the Ukhia UNO.
Local residents said the fire broke out at around 7:30am at the resort beside the Marine Drive road. Fire Service personnel rushed to the scene after receiving the alert, while local residents joined the firefighting and rescue efforts with assistance from police.
Later in the afternoon, Fire Service official Syed Morshed Hossain said 10 bodies had been recovered and warned that more victims could still be trapped inside the resort.
The rescue operation was continuing.

item.title: ULAB seminar explores UK postgraduate study options
item.description:
The Department of Media Studies and Journalism (MSJ) at the University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh (ULAB), in collaboration with education consultancy MACES, hosted a seminar on postgraduate study opportunities in the United Kingdom at the university on Wednesday.
Titled “Explore Postgraduate Study Options in Media Studies and Journalism at Prestigious UK Universities,” the seminar aimed to connect students and alumni with British academic institutions.
Representatives from 3 UK universities led interactive sessions: Tim Anderson, senior international recruitment officer at City St George’s, University of London; Isobel Hussey, senior international officer at the University of Sussex; and David Evans, regional manager at Cardiff University.
They briefed attendees on admission pathways, academic requirements, scholarship opportunities and the cultural experience of pursuing media degrees in the UK.
ULAB Vice-Chancellor Professor Shamsad Mortuza said the university was committed to providing students with greater global exposure.
“Collaborations like this seminar are instrumental in providing our students with the pathways they need to excel on the international stage. We want our graduates to not just participate in the global media discourse, but to lead it,” he said.
Attendees said direct interactions with university representatives helped clarify the application process.
Raisa Islam, a final-year MSJ student, said the session clarified specific scholarship opportunities, making the prospect of studying abroad a more achievable goal.
The event concluded with personalized question-and-answer sessions, providing aspiring media professionals with information on pursuing postgraduate studies abroad.

item.title: PM pledges to consider raising disability allowances
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Saturday said the government would consider a further increase in allowances for persons with disabilities, subject to the country's financial capacity, to help them lead more comfortable lives.
"Although we have already increased the allowances to some extent, we could not raise them as much as you needed. Insha Allah, we will increase them a little more in the future, depending on the financial capacity of the state," he said.
The prime minister told an exchange-of-views meeting with representatives of the Bangladesh Protibandhi Kallyan Samity (BPKS) at Shapla Hall of the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) in the capital.
Tarique Rahman said both the government and society had a responsibility to stand beside them and ensure their rights and dignity, acknowledging that the needs of persons with disabilities had not been adequately addressed.
"We have started working, and I cannot say how much we will be able to do. But I can assure you that you will receive our maximum support," he said.
The prime minister said building plans lacking the necessary facilities for persons with disabilities would not be approved, adding that instructions had already been issued to this effect.
The government, he said, would explore ways to introduce sign-language services at public institutions to help persons with hearing and speech impairments access essential services.
Tarique Rahman said he would ask the Law Minister to discuss the feasibility of providing sign-language assistance in courts and raise the issue with the Health Minister to explore similar arrangements in hospitals.
He asked the Social Welfare Minister to explore ways to expand skills training, including in information technology, to help persons with disabilities develop their talents and become economically self-reliant.
He also said he would discuss with the Education Ministry the possibility of creating employment opportunities for persons with disabilities in educational institutions.
The government would examine whether the age limit for persons with disabilities applying for government jobs could be extended by at least one or two years, he added.
The prime minister said he would ask the Agriculture Ministry to consider providing special support to farmers with disabilities. About public transport, he said the government would explore ways to improve the existing pink bus services for women to make them accessible to women with disabilities. The possibility of introducing disability-friendly buses in Dhaka and other major cities would also be considered, he added.
Tarique Rahman said he would instruct the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) to determine the actual number of persons with disabilities in the country so that the government could formulate appropriate policies and support measures based on reliable data.
Regarding political representation, the prime minister said he would discuss within his party the possibility of ensuring parliamentary representation for persons with disabilities along the lines of reserved seats for women.
The issue, he said, involved constitutional considerations and that he could not make a definitive statement at this stage. However, he would discuss the matter with his party colleagues and, if feasible, consider arrangements for representation by one woman and one man with disabilities.
The prime minister also referred to a memorandum of understanding involving the Ministries of Social Welfare, Law, and Women and Children Affairs on providing legal aid to persons with disabilities. He expressed hope that the initiative would help address their difficulties in accessing justice.
Reaffirming the government's commitment to supporting persons with disabilities, he said everyone had the right to live with dignity and enjoy equal rights and opportunities.
The meeting was moderated by BPKS Founder and Executive Director Abdus Sattar Dulal. Thirty persons with disabilities and representatives of disability organisations spoke at the event, highlighting their problems and placing their demands before the Prime Minister.

item.title: 17 dead, 25 hurt in stampede at India religious gathering
item.description:
At least 17 people were killed and two dozen more injured Saturday in eastern India after a stampede that was likely caused by sudden rainfall during a Hindu religious gathering, officials said.
West Bengal’s Chief Minister Suvendhu Adhikari told reporters the fatalities included a seven-year-old girl, adding that 25 others were injured outside a pavilion “in a stampede” at the Hindu festival of Durga Puja in the city of Kolkata.
“Six bodies have so far been identified,” Adhikari said.
A senior police official at the scene told AFP an announcement caused “commotion” after it started raining at night and the “crowd waiting outside the pandal (pavilion) was pushing, pulling and rushing forward and fell on the ground, leading to the stampede.”
Deadly crowd incidents are a frequent occurrence at Indian mass events, such as religious festivals, due to poor management and safety lapses.
Last year, a stampede at India’s Kumbh Mela religious fair killed 30 people and injured several others, and 11 fans were crushed to death in Bengaluru during celebrations for the local cricket team’s first Indian Premier League title.
The same year, 36 people were killed after a stampede broke out at a campaign rally of a popular actor-turned-politician in southern Tamil Nadu state.
In 2024, 121 people were killed in northern Uttar Pradesh state during a Hindu religious gathering.

item.title: Why columns matter
item.description:
One of my newspaper columns changed how the British government works.
OK, changed in a pretty small way, but change it it did.
Which is a useful answer to the question posed by HM Nazmul Alam in this newspaper .
Why do we write opinion columns, why do we bother? As we say in Britain, today's newspapers are, after all, tomorrow's wrappers for the fish and chips.
We might provide some passing amusement to readers but are we actually important? Do we change the world at all?
So, an example from my own life. My writing life if you prefer.
It's an obvious observation that there are a lot of people demanding that taxes should be higher. Usually, taxes on other people should be higher.
But there are some who insist that the government having more money would make the world a better place. So, I wondered about this. I went to the UK Treasury and asked them whether anybody had made extra, voluntary, tax payments last year because they thought this way.
That no one had asked this before became clear very quickly. For no one knew. Not only that, the Treasury itself thought the idea wholly ridiculous.
It took them a few months to find out, but eventually they were able to tell me that in the tax year 2005, there had been five voluntary donations. Donations -- four of those donating were dead, leaving bequests. From which we can derive that there was one whole person in the country of the 70 million at the time who thought that the government having more money was so important that they voluntarily sent in more tax than they had to pay.
This is not grand evidence of the desire of everyone to pay more tax, of course, despite the very high number of people who demanded that taxes should be higher.
So, I wrote my column, The Times published it in 2006. I thought it was a very good joke, and I cashed my cheque for having written it.
As far as I was concerned, that was that. Well, except for dragging that example out now and again when there was one or another group demanding that they all be taxed more. For there are such groups.
Patriotic Millionaires is one of them. Rich people who demand that they be taxed more because they're rich. To which a perfectly sensible, even sufficient, answer is that you can pay extra tax, go ahead. Isn't it amazing how none of them do?
A number of people have, over the years, repeated my column, including the numbers for different tax years. I've not been keeping track but I think I'm right in saying that never has the number gone beyond a dozen of those voluntary, extra, taxpayers.
So far so, just me and my little joke. But a few weeks back, those Patriotic Millionaires demanded, again, that they be taxed more. The answer from the government was that you can pay extra tax, if you wish, and they referred to the government webpage which explains how to do it . That response, that webpage, stems directly from that column I did two decades ago.
But is it true that writing a newspaper column can indeed change the world?
Obviously, we're not going to bring about peace, love, and understanding for all forever. But it might well be possible to make a little change, here or there.
In my professional work at a think-tank, I've been a part of more substantial changes too. But yes, columns matter. And it's not the ones we think either.
I really was trying to make a joke about the difference between the public calls and the private actions, and I was doing so in order to do nothing more than gain a few pounds sterling to spend on my own desires.
One final thing. A little thing for any journalist out there interested in finance. Repeat the article for Bangladesh. We all know -- and can probably identify -- those who insist that taxes should be higher.
So, go and ask the authorities how many people pay higher than legally demanded taxes. Find out -- how many people made donations to the government last tax year? The article comparing that to how many call for higher taxes will be published. If you really work at it, you can do it anew each year too.
No, I'll not try to charge a royalty on the idea -- I stole it from an American, about the US, in the first place. They've been running an account called “Gifts to the United States” since 1843. It's never received more than a handful of millions of dollars in any one year.
People just don't believe in higher taxes enough to pay them when they don't have to. And that? That's a really useful little lesson from a newspaper column.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.

item.title: Revenge is not a development strategy
item.description:
Two World Bank reports, published less than 11 months apart, illustrate the increasing fragility of Bangladesh's development gains.
The November 2025 Poverty and Equity Assessment documented a decline in national poverty from 37. 1% in 2010 to 18. 7% in 2022.
The Bangladesh Development Update, released on October 6, 2026, presents a troubling reversal: National poverty is estimated at 22.5% in FY 2025-26 and projected to reach 22.8% in FY 2026-27.
The latest update also estimates that approximately 2.1 million additional people fell below the international poverty line of $3 per day during FY 2025-26.
This is a distinct measure from the national poverty rate. Both indicators point to deteriorating household welfare, although neither represents a new household survey count. This distinction is important when using these figures to assess government performance.
The central question is whether Bangladesh can pursue accountability without undermining productive businesses and the livelihoods they support. When political retaliation damages factories or obstructs legitimate commerce, workers bear costs that have not been imposed by any court.
A fair assessment requires acknowledging that the crisis did not begin in August 2024. Inflation, foreign exchange shortages, and import restrictions had already weakened the economy.
Banking vulnerabilities accumulated over many years due to weak oversight, connected lending, and governance failures. The poverty assessment also found that growth had become less inclusive after 2016. Recent global energy disruptions have added further pressure.
However, inherited conditions do not absolve the government of responsibility. Governments must be assessed on whether their actions contain existing weaknesses or exacerbate them.
The World Bank identifies financial fragility, energy constraints, weak revenue mobilization, and uncertainty as obstacles to recovery. Protecting lawful business activity and maintaining public order are essential components of an effective response.
Growth slowed from 5.8% in FY 2022-23 to 4.2% in FY 2023-24, then to 3.5% in FY 2024-25, and is estimated at 3.4% in FY 2025-26. The slowdown therefore began during the Awami League regime.
Moreover, FY 2025-26 spans both the interim and the elected government, with the latter assuming office in February 2026. Attributing the entire year's performance to either administration would misrepresent the chronology.
Nevertheless, the destruction of industrial assets after August 2024 deserves direct scrutiny. The looting and arson at Gazi Tires in Rupganj on August 25, 2024 became a disturbing example of the failure to protect a business associated with a former minister.
Reports of missing people require careful investigation; they should not be presented as a confirmed death toll. The destruction itself, and its consequences for employment, are sufficient grounds for concern.
A March 5, 2025, Prothom Alo report recorded 95 permanent factory closures across major industrial areas during the preceding seven months, affecting 61,881 workers.
Its explanation extended beyond political violence: Financial distress, insufficient orders, attacks on politically-connected businesses, and owners going into hiding all contributed. The report identified 33,244 job losses across 14 factories in Beximco Industrial Park. These losses are included in the broader total and should not be counted as an additional figure.
This evidence supports criticism of inadequate protection and industrial disruption. However, it does not establish that every closure resulted from retaliation. Maintaining this distinction strengthens the argument by focusing attention on failures that authorities could reasonably have prevented or mitigated.
An owner accused of corruption should be subject to investigation, asset recovery where justified, and a fair trial. Employees, suppliers, and customers should not automatically lose their livelihoods or contracts.
Where legally permissible and commercially feasible, professional administration or restructuring can preserve a viable enterprise while the courts determine liability. These arrangements must protect creditors and prevent the concealment or diversion of assets.
Nor should the preservation of employment serve as a justification for rescuing every indebted conglomerate with public funds. Some businesses may be insolvent or reliant on privileges that cannot continue.
The objective should be orderly restructuring, transparent decision-making, and payment of workers’ lawful dues. Political identity should neither confer immunity nor substitute for evidence.
Achieving this requires decisions at the level of individual enterprises. Authorities should distinguish funds suspected of being criminal proceeds from those necessary for lawful operations. Restrictions should be justified, proportionate, and subject to review.
Workers need clear information on wages and compensation, while lenders require reliable financial statements and a viability assessment.
Without this discipline, a campaign against wrongdoing can spread losses throughout an entire supply chain and undermine confidence in legitimate enforcement.
The broader deterioration in public order reinforces this concern. In its year-end 2025 reporting, Ain o Salish Kendra recorded at least 197 deaths from mob violence during that year and reported at least 293 since the interim administration began.
The latter was a cumulative figure reported before that administration ended, not a final count for its entire tenure. These deaths demonstrate a serious failure of protection, although they cannot all be classified as political retaliation.
Human Rights Watch’s January 2025 report also documented the resurgence of abusive security practices and reprisals against individuals perceived to support the Awami League. Its warnings about arbitrary arrests and indiscriminate criminal complaints underscore the importance of due process.
Accountability loses credibility when allegations supplant investigation or when individuals are treated as guilty by association.
Economic consequences arise through identifiable channels. Damage to factories disrupts production and deliveries. Uncertain legal treatment may discourage lending and investment. Workers who lose wages reduce their spending, affecting shops, transport operators, and other local businesses.
These mechanisms provide compelling reasons to protect enterprises, although the World Bank’s aggregate figures do not quantify the distinct contribution of political retaliation.
The investment indicators are concerning. Private sector credit growth fell to its lowest level in 33 years. Net foreign direct investment declined by 15% in FY 2025-26, while new equity investment fell by 70. 3%.
Weakness in the financial sector, energy shortages, and global conditions also influence these outcomes. These figures are warning signs of a challenging investment environment, rather than evidence of a single political cause.
The earlier poverty assessment recorded nearly two million fewer employed people between 2023 and 2024 and projected a further decline of 0.8 million in 2025. That projection should not be treated as a subsequently verified outcome. Its broader message remains relevant: Weakening employment and purchasing power threaten households with limited capacity to absorb shocks.
There are also achievements to acknowledge. Remittances reached $35.6 billion in FY 2025-26, reserves improved, and average inflation eased from 10% to 8.7%.
More transparent recognition of problem loans is necessary, although the reported non-performing loan ratio of 33.2% in June 2026 demonstrates the scale of the remaining repair effort. Macroeconomic stabilization is valuable, but it must translate into productive investment and employment.
The elected government now bears responsibility for recovery. It should protect viable firms through lawful restructuring, investigate industrial arson regardless of political affiliation, and review cases through independent scrutiny of the evidence.
Bank restructuring requires credible deadlines and a fair allocation of losses. Reliable energy supply and stronger revenue collection should also form part of the recovery agenda.
Households need protection while these reforms take effect. About half of the poorest remain outside social protection programs. The World Bank estimates that consolidating food subsidies and combining the Family Card with better targeting of existing cash programs could lift millions out of poverty.
Bangladesh need not choose between justice and jobs. It must pursue justice through institutions capable of protecting both public funds and lawful livelihoods.
The promise of dignity after the uprising cannot be fulfilled if ordinary workers repeatedly bear the costs of their employers' politics.
The writer is a US-based policy analyst and freelance consultant on financial risk management.

At least 19 people were killed and two dozen more injured Saturday in Kolkata, West Bengal, India after a stampede that occurred during sudden rainfall at a Hindu religious gathering, officials and Indian media said.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressed the tragedy in a short statement on Facebook.

"The stampede in Kolkata is saddening. Condolences to the bereaved families. Wishing the injured a speedy recovery," he wrote.

"The West Bengal Government is providing all possible help to the affected families."

Adhikari originally announced 17 fatalities. The Press Trust of India (PTI) reported the death toll rose by two to 19, quoting Adhikari in a later statement.

Nine dead bodies have been released to their families, the PTI reported.

It also said police have taken the closed circuit footage of the festival and authorities would initiate action against those seen on CCTV who appeared to fail in their responsibility for crowd control.

Videos shot before the stampede appeared to show large crowds of people waiting to enter the pavilion, in an area with narrow lanes that allow only a few people to walk in at a time, according to Indian Express.

Deadly crowd incidents are a frequent occurrence at Indian mass events, such as religious festivals, due to poor management and safety lapses.

Last year, a stampede at India's Kumbh Mela religious fair killed 30 people and injured several others, and 11 fans were crushed to death in Bengaluru during celebrations for the local cricket team's first Indian Premier League title.
