item.title: Jagannath University: Questions raised over back-to-back ‘Beef Feasts’
item.description:
Jagannath University students have organised another ‘beef feast’, this time arranged by the university unit of Bangladesh Khelafat Chhatra Majlis.

Earlier on Saturday (17 October) morning, a cow was slaughtered on the road between the vice-chancellor's residence and the Mathematics Department.

Later at around 3:30 pm, beef tehari was distributed in front of the Central Shaheed Minar. The student organisation also arranged a qawwali programme on campus for the evening.

However, questions have been raised about the rationale for organising two consecutive, large-scale ‘beef feasts’, particularly during Durga Puja, the biggest religious festival of the Hindu community.

The organisers said students were charged Tk 40 each as a registration fee to participate in the programme. They bought a cow for Tk 85,000 and distributed food from 3:30 pm to 5:30 pm on Saturday. They also claimed to have arranged mutton kacchi biryani for Hindu students.

Before that, on Friday (16 October) morning, a cow was slaughtered as part of a programme titled ‘Beef Feast for Jagannath University Students’. Khichuri and beef were later distributed among students. The event was organised by the Jagannath University Central Students’ Union (JnUCSU).

A day later, the student wing of the Islamist party Bangladesh Khelafat Majlis organised another beef feast on campus.

It is worth noting that most members of JnUCSU’s elected committee, including its vice-president and general secretary, are leaders of Islami Chhatra Shibir.

Obaidul Islam, member secretary of the Jagannath University unit of Khelafat Chhatra Majlis, told Prothom Alo that food had been arranged for more than 600 people on Saturday.

He described the programme as a protest movement, saying the beef feast and qawwali event had been organised to maintain goodwill and harmony among students of all religions and viewpoints at the university.

University proctor Professor Azam Khan told Prothom Alo that although there had been objections to Friday’s programme, the event passed peacefully.

The administration was initially reluctant to permit Saturday's event organised by Khelafat Chhatra Majlis, but eventually granted approval under specific conditions.

Questions raised over ‘beef feast’

On Saturday morning, after Friday’s beef feast, writer and researcher Mohiuddin Ahmad published a satirical post on Facebook.

“The significance of slaughtering a cow with such fanfare at Jagannath University is immense. The nation will soon understand it,” he wrote.

In the post, he sarcastically listed what he said had been achieved through the event. “We have once again proved that we are an independent country by slaughtering a cow. Until now, we had not experienced the taste of true independence. If we cannot slaughter a cow at a university, what kind of independence is that?” he wrote.

Mohammad Tanzimuddin Khan, a professor in the Department of International Relations at the University of Dhaka, sees an expression of religious hostility in the organisation of beef feasts at Jagannath University.

“The values of students need to be clear. An event that creates fear among people from another community should not be organised,” he told Prothom Alo.

He noted that the true intent behind such actions is to perpetuate a culture of fear and assert dominance on campus, adding that whether acts creating fear in others belong on a university campus must be questioned.

Shamsul Arefin, member secretary of the Jagannath University unit of Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal, told Prothom Alo that the situation should be brought under control through consensus and cooperation from everyone, without any provocation.

“Everyone should have thought about this before organising such an event during the biggest festival of the Hindu community. Ensuring the safety of minorities is everyone’s responsibility,” he said.

Ivan Tahseeb, president of the Jagannath University unit of Socialist Students’ Front, told Prothom Alo that cows were slaughtered during Eid, but slaughtering a cow during another religion’s festival had put the organisers in a difficult position.

Using an issue such as personal freedom to create communal tension on campus is unacceptable, he added.

How the ‘beef feast’ controversy began

On the night of 12 October, students from the 2021–22 academic session of the university’s Department of Islamic History and Culture arranged to cook beef khichuri near the campus’s Muktamancha. The university’s central temple is located close to the site.

Several Hindu students objected to the cooking arrangement. They alleged that cooking beef in front of the temple had hurt their religious sentiments. There were also allegations that bricks from the temple had been used to build the makeshift cooking stoves. Hindu students subsequently staged protests on campus over the incident.

On 14 October, the university’s proctor’s office issued a notice asking people to refrain from slaughtering animals on campus. The notice cited the need to protect public health and maintain cleanliness and a hygienic environment. It also said action could be taken in accordance with a public notice issued by Dhaka South City Corporation if the directive was violated.

JnUCSU strongly opposed the directive, holding a protest march and rally on Wednesday night. They put forward a four-point charter of demands—withdrawing the notice, issuing a public apology, investigating the incident, serving beef and mutton in the university cafeteria and ensuring religious harmony.

The university administration later issued an official statement saying everyone had the right to slaughter animals and organise events on campus. However, it said all concerned should ensure that no event disrupted another person’s programme or activities.

The statement added that the proctor had requested people to refrain from slaughtering animals to prevent unwanted tension and a deterioration in religious harmony amid the recent situation.

The administration expressed regret that the request had led to misunderstandings.

item.title: Mass protests in France spiral into worst riots in years
item.description:
FRANCE-SOCIAL-DEMO

Rioting erupted in cities across France on Saturday as demonstrations against rising living costs and declining public services spiralled out of control in some of the worst violence the country has witnessed for decades.

While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully in street marches in scores of cities, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers.

In Limoges, the city hall was set ablaze; in Marseille, black-clad protesters broke into city hall and defaced the building with anarchic graffiti, and in Lyon, protesters torched the city's tourist office.

French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the government would not be "intimidated" by violence, and blamed the unrest on the "ultra-left" and criminals just months before a presidential election next year.

"To those who clearly want to use this violence as a 'warm-up' before the presidential election, I say clearly: We will not let ourselves be intimidated. No one will impose their political agenda through violence," he wrote in a post on X.

Some 1,200 people had been arrested as part of the protests, Lecornu added while visiting the sites in the evening.

Around 550,000 people had participated in the demonstrations across the country, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said. The CGT union told Reuters it estimated protesters at 800,000 people.

President Emmanuel Macron vowed to prosecute and punish people who had carried out the attacks.

"We will all stand united against the sowers of chaos, who only seek to undermine our institutions and prevent those who peacefully express their demands from doing so," he wrote in a post on X.

Belgium, Portugal and Italy also faced smaller-scale protests on Saturday as living costs rise in Europe, while protesters in Albania again rallied against perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards.

Protesters said most people had marched peacefully, and put much of the violence down to troublemakers who had set out to cause damage and clash with the police. Many held signs bearing slogans against the police, the president and the wealthy.

"We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions," said Lola, a 19-year-old protester in Paris.

Tear Gas, Fire and Looting

Most protests kicked off around midday, with some beginning before the official start of the demonstrations.

In some parts of Paris, police fired tear gas rounds as they retreated in the face of mostly young protesters, many of whom were dressed in black and wore hoodies, masks and goggles to protect against tear gas.

Rioters tried to break into the Galeries Lafayette department store, smashed up banks, ransacked a Lacoste store as well as other boutiques and looted an SFR mobile phone shop. Protesters had been setting objects ablaze all day, including numerous cars.

In protests partly inspired by those in France, several hundred mostly young people protested in Brussels, and some clashed with police. Belgian student groups have said they are protesting against rising education costs and reforms they fear will make higher education less accessible.

In Albania, police fired what appeared to be rubber bullets at protesters during a fifth day of mass student demonstrations calling for Prime Minister Edi Rama to step down.

In Portugal, tens of thousands took to the streets of Lisbon following days of unrest to protest against housing and other living costs. Housing prices in Portugal have doubled since 2017, fuelling one of the worst affordability crises in Europe.

In Italy, a march against high costs of living in Milan degenerated into disorder, with police clearing the central cathedral square with tear gas. Police in Bologna used water cannons to try to disperse crowds and made seven arrests after another protest turned violent, the ANSA news agency reported.

French Police Response under Scrutiny

The protests in France began last ‌month at high schools in Paris' working-class northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved into a broader movement focused on inequality, public spending and living standards.

In Paris on Saturday, protesters in high-visibility vests blocked streets, recalling the Yellow Vest movement that marked Macron's previous term in office.

Saturday's protests eclipsed the size of the crowds at the peak of the Yellow Vest movement, though they were far lower than the levels seen at the protests in 2023 against Macron's pension overhaul.

Macron is entering the final stretch of his presidency, facing a fragmented political landscape and growing pressure over the economy.

France's efforts to reduce public debt have not reassured investors, pushing government borrowing costs to their highest levels in over two decades.

Police tactics have drawn criticism following injuries among demonstrators, including a teenager who lost a hand after picking up a stun grenade. The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence.

Lecornu said more than 150 police officers had been injured in Saturday's protests, but did not say whether any protesters had been hurt.

Nunez confirmed reports that one person had his hand torn off in clashes with police on Saturday. French media reported he tried to pick up a stun grenade.

The UNSA police union posted a video on X showing crowds attacking police vans with clubs and bricks in multiple locations. The union warned the government police forces were at breaking point.

"Today again, in every corner of France, our colleagues are being used as punching bags. Pelted with stones, injured, trapped in real ambushes," the union said. "Let everyone take responsibility: this cannot go on indefinitely. The rope is stretched to its maximum."

item.title: Bangladesh suffer 99-run defeat to Zimbabwe in tri-nation series opener
item.description:
Bangladesh suffered a 99-run defeat to Zimbabwe in the opening match of the tri-nation series in Abu Dhabi on Saturday, being bowled out for 172 while chasing a target of 272.

The loss once again exposed Bangladesh’s struggles with the bat in one-day cricket.

Bangladesh made a promising start to the chase, scoring 42 without losing a wicket in the first six overs. However, Soumya Sarkar’s dismissal triggered a collapse, leaving Bangladesh unable to recover as wickets fell at regular intervals.

Zimbabwe’s bowling was not particularly outstanding, but Bangladesh’s batters repeatedly gave their wickets away. Towhid Hridoy, Najmul Hossain and Mosaddek Hossain, who were expected to steady the innings in the middle overs, were all dismissed leg-before wicket after misjudging the line of the ball.

Tanzid Hasan, who had been dropped on the previous delivery, gave away his wicket with a catch on the very next ball. Soumya Sarkar was caught in the slips.

Earlier, Zimbabwe posted 271 for eight in their 50 overs, with Craig Ervine scoring 93 and Brendan Taylor making 81. Ervine was named player of the match. Taskin Ahmed took three wickets for Bangladesh, while Saif Hassan and Shoriful Islam claimed two each.

Tanzid top-scored for Bangladesh with 46, while Saif made 26 and Rishad Hossain added 23. For Zimbabwe, Brad Evans took four wickets for 45 runs, while Sikandar Raza and Masakadza claimed two wickets each.

Bangladesh will face Afghanistan in their next match on 21 October. To reach the final, they must win that match and rely on other results going their way.

Bangladesh will be hoping Zimbabwe beat Afghanistan in their match tomorrow. If that happens, the next match could effectively become a semi-final.

Brief scores

Zimbabwe: 271/8 in 50 overs (Craig Ervine 93, Brendan Taylor 81, Nyamhuri 21 not out; Taskin Ahmed 3/44, Saif Hassan 2/17, Shoriful Islam 2/47).

Bangladesh: 172 all out in 33.4 overs (Tanzid Hasan 46, Saif Hassan 26, Rishad Hossain 23; Brad Evans 4/45, Sikandar Raza 2/28, Masakadza 2/18).

Result: Zimbabwe won by 99 runs.

Player of the match: Craig Ervine.

item.title: Messi brace lifts Inter Miami to 3-1 win in Atlanta
item.description:
FOC-MLS-SOC-SPO-ATLANTA-UNITED-FC-V-INTER-MIAMI-CF

Lionel Messi scored twice in the space of four minutes to lift Inter Miami to a 3-1 victory at Atlanta United on Saturday as the Herons' MLS title defense continued to gain steam with the playoffs approaching.

The 39-year-old superstar tops the Major League Soccer scoring chart with 25 goals, six ahead of Croatian striker Petar Musa of FC Dallas and Philadelphia's Milan Iloski.

At the same Atlanta stadium where Messi helped Argentina beat England in the World Cup semi-finals in July, Messi delivered two scintillating goals to secure Miami's third straight victory.

German Berterame, who put Miami up 1-0 in the 45th minute, turned provider, finding Messi who weaved through the Atlanta defense to unleash a left footed shot from the center of the box and make it 2-0 in the 56th minute.

Four minutes later Messi struck again, breaking away on a pass from Luis Suarez and getting the better of hapless Junior Alonso to fire past Atlanta keeper Lucas Hoyos.

Messi had helped put Miami on top shortly before halftime, heading the ball to Suarez who shook off his defender in the box and lofted a pass that Berterame nodded home to make it 1-0.

Messi was credited with an assist, that saw him pull level with LAFC's Son Heung-min atop the assists table. Messi is the first player in MLS history to record at least 15 assists in three straight seasons.

Messi now has four goals in three matches since his emotional Argentina send-off. Miami, who clinched a playoff berth on Wednesday, won their third straight game under Cristian "Kily" Gonzalez, who took over as coach last month.

Fafa Picault converted a penalty in the 89th minute to pull a goal back for Atlanta, but at second-from-bottom in the Eastern Conference Gerardo Martino's team are running out of time to turn things around in time to reach the playoffs.

item.title: Press freedom essential to attracting foreign investment
item.description:
Joerd Sjoerdsma, the Netherlands’ Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation, has stressed the importance of ensuring democratic stability and press freedom to attract foreign investment to Bangladesh. He made the remarks during a brief, one-day visit to Dhaka on Tuesday, while speaking to Prothom Alo and several other media outlets.

According to Sjoerdsma, Dutch companies want to invest more in Bangladesh, but certain non-tariff barriers need to be removed. Ensuring workers’ rights is also essential to advancing trade relations between Bangladesh and the European Union (EU). He believes Bangladesh’s economy has considerable potential.

Asked about the relationship between democracy, press freedom and foreign investment in Bangladesh, Sjoerdsma said, “If you want to have a stable business environment and if you want Dutch businesses to come to Bangladesh a stable democracy and also freedom of press are crucial. That means they know the investment will be safe. If you look at Dutch investors if you look at Dutch business people they look at the whole picture.”

Drawing on his country’s experience of press freedom, the Dutch minister said, “I think in general, in the Netherlands, we are used to free press and also press that sometimes ask very critical questions. And I may not like this as a minister, but sometimes these questions have the right basis and I really have to answer to them. The same holds true for my position in Parliament. Parliament may be critical I have to answer to them.”

Democracy, economic progress must go hand in hand

Sjoerdsma views Bangladesh’s recent political changes and the national election in February positively. He said, “We were heartened by the way the election was conducted in February to see a major transition in the society in Bangladesh. To see the rise of democratic governance and of course we've spoken about this today with various cabinet ministers including the Prime Minister and they told us that they view it's crucial to continue to implement the reforms on democratic governance.”

Sjoerdsma added, “And we've also spoken to civil society and they urged us please make sure that they follow through and I have the feeling that there's this sense of urgency that this will happen.”

“But the same is true for the economy. It's crucial to do both transitions at the same time, a transition to a full democracy, and a transition to a wealthy and prosperous economy. And I think on both sides of the road the Netherlands stands ready to be a strategic partner of Bangladesh. But, of course it also requires the political will of the cabinet of Bangladesh,” the Dutch minister said.

When asked whether he was satisfied with Bangladesh’s political and economic environment following the election, Sjoerdsma said the current situation had created many opportunities. Stability was becoming evident, he said, adding that Bangladesh had held a free and fair election and that the new government was open to business and welcoming investors.

Emphasising the need for continuity in implementing reforms, the Dutch minister said reforms could not be completed in a day. Even after they were introduced, they had to be implemented every day. This required long-term efforts and cooperation, he added.

Workers’ rights are important

Speaking about future trade relations between Bangladesh and the EU, Sjoerdsma said workers’ rights would have to be respected for the two sides to conclude a free trade agreement.

He said the Netherlands believed that reaching a free trade agreement between the EU and Bangladesh as soon as possible was extremely important, and that his country was pressing for such an agreement.

“We are moving rapidly towards a trade agreement, but we must also ensure that the remaining challenges, including non-tariff barriers, are addressed as quickly as possible,” Sjoerdsma said.

item.title: Written contracts for leaked job exam questions at Tk 1 million
item.description:
Applicants had to pay Tk 1 million to obtain the questions and answers for a recruitment examination. Those interested in the deal had to submit their original academic certificates, which would not be returned until the full amount was paid. Applicants unable to pay upfront had to provide signed bank cheques worth Tk 200,000 to Tk 300,000.

Members of the gang arrested over the leak of questions for the recruitment examination for assistant youth development officers at the Department of Youth Development used to enter into written agreements with jobseekers under these terms, according to officials involved in the investigation. They told Prothom Alo about the arrangement based on information obtained during interrogation of the arrested suspects.

The Special Response Battalion (SRB) arrested seven members of the gang during raids in and outside Dhaka from Wednesday to Friday. The authorities seized 116 Tk 100 stamp papers, 10 academic certificates belonging to jobseekers, cheque leaves belonging to 40 people and bank cheque books.

The arrested individuals are Nur Mohammad, 30, an office assistant at the National Board of Revenue (NBR); Md Jahangir, 38, and SM Imdadul Islam, 35, computer operators; Asadul Islam, 33, an office assistant at the Ministry of Defence; Md Rubel Islam, 33, a data entry operator at the Department of Environment; and two other gang members, Mofizul Islam, 23, and Md Hasinur Rahman, also known as Sujon. They were sent to jail through a court order yesterday.

Tk 1 million agreements on stamp papers

Lieutenant Colonel Faizul Arefin, commander of SRB-3, said the unit was conducting a shadow investigation into the case filed with Motijheel police station over the leak of questions for the preliminary recruitment examination for assistant youth development officers at the Department of Youth Development.

He said gang members signed written agreements with jobseekers on stamp papers for Tk 1 million in exchange for providing the examination questions and answers.

The applicants’ original academic certificates were kept in the gang members’ custody until the full amount was paid. Under the terms of the agreements, candidates could retrieve their certificates only after paying the entire sum.

Those unable to pay the amount upfront were required to hand over signed bank cheque leaves. Each cheque was filled out for an amount ranging from Tk 200,000 to Tk 300,000, Lieutenant Colonel Faizul Arefin said.

Another SRB official told Prothom Alo that the gang members had collected signed bank cheques worth Tk 200,000 to Tk 300,000 from at least 40 jobseekers.

Investigators are examining how and from whom the leaked questions reached the gang members. Efforts are underway to identify others involved in the incident and bring them to justice, the official said.

Answers circulated through NBR employees

According to investigators, after the question paper was leaked, answers were prepared and circulated among other members of the gang. They subsequently passed the answer sheets on to prospective examinees and people who had purchased the leaked questions.

Faizul Arefin said the answers to the leaked questions were circulated among other gang members through employees of the NBR.

According to information from investigation sources, NBR office assistant Nur Mohammad received a blurry photograph of the question paper on his mobile phone at 4:43am on 10 October. At around 6:15am, Jahangir, a computer operator at the same organisation, received a clearer photograph of the same question paper.

The answers were then prepared and sent to other members of the gang, who passed them on to prospective examinees and buyers of the leaked questions.

Case to be transferred to CID

Mohammad Harun-or-Rashid, deputy commissioner of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police’s Motijheel division, said a decision had been made to transfer the case filed with Motijheel police station over the question leak to the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) of police.

Investigation officer Mirza Mohammad Mukta said the case documents would be handed over to the CID on Sunday.

The Ministry of Youth and Sports formed a five-member committee on Saturday to investigate the alleged question leak. The committee, headed by an additional secretary to the ministry, has yet to submit its report.

Meanwhile, the recruitment examination was held again on Friday.

The preliminary examination for the recruitment of assistant youth development officers at the Department of Youth Development had originally been scheduled for 10 October. A total of 318,976 candidates were deemed eligible to compete for 242 vacant posts.

According to the original schedule, the multiple-choice examination was to be held at 10 educational institutions across Dhaka city from 11am to noon that day. However, reports of the question leak emerged before the examination began. After confirming the leak at 10:03am, the authorities postponed the examination.

The following day, 11 October, Md Atikur Rahman, deputy director (administration) of the Department of Youth Development, filed a case with Motijheel police station over the incident

item.title: Ashulia’s toxic burden: Workers face growing environmental health crisis
item.description:
For thousands of workers and residents living beside Bangladesh’s rapidly expanding textile and industrial belt, pollution is no longer an abstract environmental issue. It is becoming a daily health reality.

Factories provide employment, income and foreign exchange for the country, but in communities surrounding the industrial centres of Ashulia and Savar, the environmental cost of production is increasingly visible.

Rivers and canals receive industrial discharges, agricultural soils are exposed to contaminated water and sediments, and communities living close to factories face repeated exposure to substances that can persist in the environment and accumulate in people.

A new community-based monitoring study conducted by the Environment and Social Development Organization (ESDO) in cooperation with Health and Environment Justice Support (HEJSupport), under a multi-actor partnership involving FEMNET, Südwind, INKOTA, BILS and other partners, has brought this hidden crisis into sharper focus. The study analysed soil, water, wastewater and human-hair samples and combined laboratory findings with interviews and focus-group discussions involving affected communities. (HEJ-Support)

The findings are deeply concerning. The research identified PFAS, chlorinated paraffins, nonylphenols, heavy metals and other hazardous chemicals in environmental samples collected from textile-producing communities in Ashulia. PFAS contamination in some water samples was extraordinarily high compared with international drinking-water benchmarks. PFOA was detected at concentrations of 2.13 and 2.99 micrograms per litre, while PFOS reached 2.78 micrograms per litre.

Compared with the US Environmental Protection Agency's current drinking-water limits cited in the report, some of these concentrations were hundreds of times higher. (HEJ-Support)

These represent a warning about the environmental conditions in which workers, children, women and other residents are living.

Chemical pollution in Bangladesh threatens public health and climate resilience

A chemical cocktail in the environment

PFAS, or per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, are often described as “forever chemicals” because many of them are highly persistent in the environment. They have been widely used because of their resistance to water, grease, heat and stains and can be associated with industrial and textile applications.

The Ashulia study found multiple PFAS compounds in tested samples. PFOA and PFOS were among those detected at particularly alarming concentrations. PFNA was also found at a level substantially above the US EPA benchmark cited by the researchers. (HEJ-Support)

The significance of PFAS contamination is that these substances do not behave like ordinary pollutants that simply disappear after entering the environment. Their persistence means contamination can remain for long periods, potentially moving through water, soil and biological systems.

The study also detected short-chain chlorinated paraffins (SCCPs). One wastewater sample contained SCCPs at 65.83 micrograms per litre, almost three times the 25 micrograms-per-litre ZDHC wastewater limit referenced in the report. Chlorinated paraffins are persistent industrial chemicals and some have serious environmental and health implications. (HEJ-Support)
Another troubling finding concerned nonylphenols and related chemicals.

Nonylphenol was detected at 76.43 micrograms per litre, more than 250 times the EU drinking-water value cited by the researchers. Octylphenol and nonylphenol ethoxylates were also detected above the referenced ZDHC limit. These substances are of particular concern because some alkylphenols have endocrine-disrupting properties. (HEJ-Support)

The picture emerging from these results is a chemical mixture problem.

Lead in the soil, mercury in human hair

The study's findings on heavy metals are equally disturbing.
Lead was detected in Ashulia agricultural soil at 114.64 parts per million, exceeding the Bangladesh agricultural soil safety threshold of 100 ppm cited in the report. Cadmium was also detected at 2.1 ppm, approaching the national agricultural threshold of 3 ppm. (HEJ-Support)

Lead contamination is particularly worrying where agricultural land, homes and industrial areas exist side by side. Lead is a potent neurotoxic substance, with children especially vulnerable to its effects. Persistent exposure can affect neurological development and other aspects of health.

The implications extend beyond the soil itself. Where contaminated soil is used for cultivation, there is a potential pathway from industrial pollution to soil, crops, livestock, food and ultimately people. Earlier research in an industrially affected agricultural area of Ashulia has also documented elevated concentrations of several heavy metals, including chromium, arsenic and lead, and identified anthropogenic activities as important sources of some of these contaminants. (PubMed Central (PMC))

Perhaps one of the most striking findings of the ESDO-HEJSupport study came from human hair analysis. Some residents had elevated mercury concentrations, with the report noting particularly concerning findings among women. Mercury is a toxic metal capable of affecting the nervous system and other biological systems. Finding elevated mercury in human biological samples does not, by itself, establish that a particular factory caused an individual's exposure or illness. But it is an important warning sign that warrants detailed exposure assessment, medical investigation and stronger environmental controls.

Health complaints are being heard

Communities are not talking only about polluted rivers and contaminated soil. Residents report health problems including respiratory difficulties, skin problems, gastrointestinal complaints, headaches, eye irritation and chronic fatigue. (femnet.de)

People living and working in industrial areas can be exposed to numerous hazards at the same time, including chemical substances, dust, fumes, poor air quality, heat, noise, unsafe working conditions and inadequate sanitation.

That is precisely why the findings demand a comprehensive environmental-health response rather than a narrow factory-by-factory inspection. The central concern is cumulative exposure.

A garment worker may spend eight to ten hours inside a factory and then return to a home located beside a polluted canal or industrial drain. A child may play near contaminated soil. A household may depend on groundwater. A farmer may irrigate crops with polluted surface water. Livestock may drink from contaminated water bodies. In such circumstances, occupational exposure and community exposure overlap.
FEMNET has noted that many people in textile-producing communities live immediately beside factories, contaminated drains and water bodies, while many also work in the textile industry themselves, creating the possibility of exposure both at work and at home. (femnet.de)

More than an environmental problem

The Ashulia-Savar crisis should therefore be understood as an environmental justice issue.

The people most exposed to industrial pollution are often not those who benefit most from the economic value generated by industrial production. Workers produce garments for domestic and international markets, while neighbouring communities absorb part of the environmental burden.
This raises a fundamental question: Who pays for the pollution?

If hazardous chemicals are discharged into waterways, the cost does not disappear. It is transferred from the factory balance sheet to the river, the farmer, the worker, the household and ultimately the public-health system.
A polluted canal may reduce the availability of clean water. Contaminated soil can undermine agriculture. Chemical exposure can create health costs. Lost working days reduce household income. Medical treatment creates additional financial pressure. Environmental degradation can also reduce the quality of life and long-term economic resilience of communities.
In other words, pollution is not free.

The burden on tens of thousands of people

The industrial belt of Ashulia and Savar is home to a very large population of workers and residents, and the affected communities identified by the study include areas such as Dhamsona, Ghoshbag, Noyapara, Jamgora, Molla Bazaar and surrounding industrial communities. The scale of the population exposed to industrial environmental pressures means that the issue cannot be treated as a small localised pollution incident. (HEJ-Support)

For tens of thousands of people living and working in and around these communities, environmental quality is directly connected to everyday survival.

Clean water is essential for drinking, cooking, washing and agriculture. Clean soil is essential for food production. Clean air is essential for workers and children. When all three environmental compartments are under pressure simultaneously, the risk becomes multidimensional.

This is why the government, industry and international brands cannot view chemical management as merely a compliance exercise.

Community-based monitoring changes the conversation

One of the most important aspects of the ESDO-HEJSupport research is its community-based monitoring approach.

Instead of relying exclusively on conventional regulatory inspections, the project incorporated observations and experiences from people who live and work in the affected areas. Environmental samples were collected and subjected to laboratory testing, while interviews and focus groups documented community experiences and health concerns. (HEJ-Support)
This approach gives communities something they have often lacked: evidence.

For years, residents may say that water has changed colour, fish have disappeared, crops are declining or people are becoming sick. Without scientific evidence, such concerns can easily be dismissed.
Laboratory results change that equation.

When community observations are combined with scientifically analysed samples, environmental complaints can become measurable evidence that regulators, factory owners, brands and policymakers must address.

What must happen now?

The first priority should be an independent and comprehensive environmental-health investigation covering the major industrial clusters of Ashulia and Savar.

Sampling should not be limited to factory wastewater outlets. It should cover rivers, canals, groundwater, agricultural soils, sediments, air, food pathways and, where ethically and medically appropriate, biological samples from exposed populations.

Second, Bangladesh needs stronger control over the use and discharge of hazardous chemicals in the textile sector. Factories should maintain transparent chemical inventories and adopt safer alternatives wherever possible.

Third, industrial wastewater treatment systems must be independently verified. Merely possessing an effluent treatment plant cannot be considered sufficient. The question is whether the plant is properly operated, whether it removes hazardous chemicals and whether treated effluent remains within applicable standards.

Fourth, workers need stronger right-to-know protections. Employees should know what chemicals they handle, what risks those substances pose and what protective measures are required.

Fifth, the government should establish systematic health surveillance for workers and communities in heavily industrialised zones. Particular attention should be given to children, pregnant women, agricultural workers and people with prolonged occupational exposure.

Sixth, international apparel brands and buyers must accept responsibility throughout their supply chains. Environmental due diligence cannot stop at the factory gate. If a brand profits from production in a particular community, its responsibility should extend to identifying and addressing serious environmental and human-rights risks associated with that production.

Development cannot be built on contamination

Bangladesh's garment industry is a national economic success story. Millions of people depend on it, directly and indirectly. Protecting workers and communities from toxic chemicals is therefore not an argument against industrialisation or exports. It is an argument for responsible industrialisation.

Economic development that destroys rivers, contaminates soil and exposes workers to hazardous chemicals is ultimately self-defeating. The country cannot protect its export competitiveness by externalising environmental and health costs onto workers and communities.
The findings from Ashulia should therefore be treated as a warning, not merely another environmental report.

PFAS hundreds of times above international drinking-water benchmarks, lead above the cited national agricultural soil threshold, mercury detected at elevated levels in human hair, and a range of other hazardous chemicals appearing in water, wastewater and soil together tell a compelling story: the chemical footprint of textile production is reaching beyond factory walls.

The people of Ashulia and Savar should not have to choose between employment and health, between economic opportunity and clean water, or between a thriving textile industry and a safe environment.

The challenge now is to ensure that Bangladesh''s industrial future does not repeat the mistakes of industrialisation elsewhere, where pollution was treated as the inevitable price of development. It is not inevitable.

With stronger regulation, cleaner production, transparent chemical management, responsible global supply chains, independent monitoring and meaningful participation by workers and communities, Ashulia can become an example of how industrial growth and environmental protection can coexist.

That transformation must begin with recognition of the problem. And the evidence emerging from the communities of Ashulia and Savar suggests that the time for recognition has already arrived.

* Dr. Shahriar Hossain is an environmental scientist and social justice advocate working on environmental pollution, toxic chemicals, public health and sustainable development.

item.title: Reforms must be carried out in our own interests, not under pressure
item.description:
Mohammed Abu Eusuf is an economist and professor in the Development Studies Department at the University of Dhaka. He is serving as the Executive Director of Research and Policy Integration for Development (RAPID). He spoke with Prothom Alo about the development and poverty situation in Bangladesh, ways for economic recovery, and reforms in the banking and revenue sectors. Monoj Dey took the interview.

The World Bank's recently published report indicates that 62 million people are in such a vulnerable state that a single economic shock could push them below the poverty line. What is the fundamental flaw in our development narrative?

Mohammed Abu Eusuf: When we talk about the development of any country, two things are of utmost importance—political stability and economic stability. Bangladesh has finally been taken over by a democratic government after a long time. We hope this will bring about political stability in the country. Now, the most critical need is to ensure economic stability.

After 5 August 2024, during the interim government period, uncertainty arose among domestic and foreign investors and businessmen due to political changes and various crises. They lacked confidence regarding the direction of the nation's economy and the investment environment. Previously, the COVID pandemic, followed by several wars and international crises, also impacted the economy. Immediately after the new government took over, various global crises, including the Iran-US war, arose. As Bangladesh is an importing country, these situations affected our economy.

Continued high inflation in Bangladesh has reduced the real purchasing power of low and limited-income people. Besides the poor and extremely poor populations, families who are ''vulnerable non-poor'' just above the poverty line are also at risk. Economic shocks or disasters may push them back below the poverty line. To tackle this situation, alongside controlling inflation, it is essential to increase wages and real income.

It is also crucial to make development inclusive. Government borrowing should not crowd out funding in the private sector. Ensuring youth employment, skill development, and an investment-friendly environment will transform political changes into sustainable economic and social progress.

Following the World Bank, the IMF''s reports also indicate that poverty will increase in the country, and GDP growth will slow down. How likely do you see the economy recovering in the next couple of years?

Mohammad Abu Eusuf: There is considerable potential for our economy to recover. The government mentioned ten priorities in the budget speech. They spoke about honest and capable leadership and accountable institutions and mentioned employment, investment, and single-window services. Now, effective steps need to be taken on these matters.
It is true that we cannot control global realities like wars and pandemics. But we have to adequately address those aspects that are within our control. Projects that are supposed to be completed in three years should indeed be completed in three years. If time and cost are increased, the extra burden ultimately falls on everyone.

If you had to specify, what should be our steps for economic recovery?

Mohammad Abu Eusuf: For economic recovery, we need a big push or a major boost. I want to explain this using the three ''C''s.

Firstly, comprehensiveness or an overall perspective. If we think about the banking sector or revenue sector in isolation, desired results will not be achieved. Because one sector is interconnected with another, we need to develop an integrated and coordinated system. For instance, in revenue collection, an automated system needs to be carried out from start to finish. For example, if we cannot connect the holding number information of the City Corporation with the relevant database to increase revenue collection, the desired outcome will not be achieved.

Secondly, coordination. There needs to be effective coordination between various government agencies. Often, WASA's work does not coordinate with the work of the power department, resulting in repeated digging in the same area, increased costs, and inconvenience for people. The initiative to bring investment-related agencies under an integrated framework is a positive step.

Thirdly, compliance. In today's world, a strong saying prevails, ''No compliance, no business.'' In the matter of compliance, there is no room for laxity in areas where we say zero tolerance. Be it environmental, social, or economic compliance, it must be ensured.

To bring about economic recovery, the three ''C''s must be ensured together. If we can ensure good governance and strengthen institutions, the path to economic recovery will become smooth. Our main issue is that while there are rules, they are not implemented. Let me give an example. The Public Money and Budget Management Act of 2009 requires the presentation of budget progress to Parliament every three months.

However, without proper implementation, it's impossible to understand where the economy is headed or what progress is being made in budget implementation.

After assuming responsibility, the current government has formulated a five-year reform strategy. It has set targets for GDP growth rate, public and private investment, and national savings. Now the question is, are we following this strategy? How can that be determined? For this, an integrated dashboard can be created, where progress based on KPIs can be measured. It needs to be considered a national priority. If progress is made according to the target in any area, it should be indicated in green, and if not, it should be shown in red. This will make it easy to identify problem areas and hold the relevant people accountable.

Banking sector reform is critical to restoring confidence in the economy. What is the way forward for reforming this sector?

Mohammad Abu Eusuf: Currently, there are 61-62 banks, which is more than in many countries. Many banks have been approved based on political considerations, which now needs to be managed by the government and the people. Recently, the governor of Bangladesh Bank had a meeting with economists and private sector representatives. There, the governor said that no bank directors would be appointed based on political considerations. This is a positive initiative, but ensuring its implementation will be the main challenge.

The bank's money belongs to depositors and customers. Restoring the confidence of depositors, businesses, and taxpayers in the banking sector is crucial to moving the economy away from its current state. Supervision of government banks is done by the Financial Institutions Division of the Ministry of Finance, while private banks are supervised by Bangladesh Bank. Discussions are also underway on whether this dual administrative system can be removed and supervision responsibilities coordinated. Such reforms are necessary to bring discipline to the banking sector. Reforms must be made in our interest, not under pressure from the IMF or the World Bank.

To bring discipline back to the banking sector, tough decisions need to be taken. If necessary, and if the situation demands it, the government must take a firm stance to close one or two banks, ensuring the protection of depositors' interests. In this case, the ''carrot and stick'' policy must be followed. Reward for good work, punishment for irregularities. Those borrowers who repay their loan installments regularly should be incentivised. Those who face difficulties in repayment due to global situations or unavoidable reasons should be assisted. However, no concession can be given to willful defaulters to save the banking sector. Granting special concessions or opportunities for evading responsibility to them will be an injustice to regular payers.

The issue of loan recovery being hindered due to long-pending cases and stays in financial loan courts must also be addressed. A special tribunal can be formed to finish trials of willful defaulters' cases within six months. Exemplary punishment will serve as a warning to others. There is no alternative to reform to restore discipline in the banking sector. A strong political will is needed irrespective of party affiliation.

Prothom Alo: Inflation has been high for over four years in the country. Why aren't the conventional tools to control inflation in Bangladesh effective?

Mohammad Abu Eusuf: There are three areas in controlling inflation. Firstly, monetary policy. The central bank has tried to control inflation by increasing the policy rate.

Secondly, revenue policy. The government reduces tariffs or provides subsidies on many imported goods. However, if its benefits are not reflected in the market, the purpose of the initiative is not fulfilled. For example, even though the government set the price of LPG gas, it is being sold at a higher price in the market. This means there is a weakness in market supervision. The government loses revenue, but the public does not receive benefits.

Thirdly, market management. In a report in Prothom Alo, it was mentioned that Malta is being imported at Tk 87, but sold in the market for Tk 500. Including duties and other expenses, its price should be a maximum of Tk 250 to Tk 300. However, due to repeated handovers and extortion, the price increases abnormally.

Two to three days of market operation is not enough to establish discipline. A continuous monitoring system must be developed throughout the year. Local administration, local government, and market committees must be involved to ensure accountability. Extortion must be stopped. The supply chain from producer to consumer must be kept normal so that intermediaries cannot make excessive profits.

One thing to remember is that ordinary people do not use 200-300 types of products. Their daily demand is focused mainly on certain essential food and essential products. If production and potential shortages of essential products like rice, oil, potatoes, and onions are determined and monitored throughout the year, it is possible to control inflation.

If India or Sri Lanka can keep inflation between 3 to 5 per cent, why can't we? Effective application, continuous monitoring, and accountability can also control inflation in Bangladesh.

Income and wealth disparity in Bangladesh is continually increasing. In 2022, based on the Gini coefficient, Bangladesh stands at the extreme of an unequal country. Where does the situation stand four years later?

Mohammad Abu Eusuf: The first thing is that the household income and expenditure survey needs to be done regularly. Now, standing in 2026, we are talking about 2022 data. Updated information is needed for effective policy formulation.

According to government figures, poverty stood at 18. 7 per cent in 2022. However, the recent World Bank estimate suggests it has risen above 22 per cent. Meanwhile, the Gini coefficient is increasing. This means that despite reducing poverty, income inequality is continuously increasing. The top 10 per cent of people have 41 per cent of total income. In terms of wealth, a large amount of wealth is concentrated in the top 1 per cent.

To reduce income inequality, we need to bring changes to our tax structure. In an economy worth 500 billion dollars, only 4. 2 to 4. 3 million tax returns are filed yearly. A large portion of this is again from government and private sector employees. In many instances, zero-return statements are being filed. Therefore, it is crucial to expand the tax base without imposing a new burden on regular taxpayers.

For example, if only ownership information related to flats and plots in major cities like Dhaka and Chittagong can be interconnected with the National Board of Revenue's (NBR) database, it is possible to significantly increase the number of taxpayers. Additionally, transparency in transactions and tax evasion can be reduced by implementing cashless transactions and Bangla QR codes in rural areas. Alongside this, an automated system must be in place from start to finish in NBR activities. If the loopholes in VAT collection can be sealed, revenue collection could increase two to three-fold.

Our economy is still heavily reliant on indirect taxes like VAT and import duties. This dependence must be reduced, and the scope of direct taxes expanded. At least one crore capable taxpayers should be targeted to bring within the tax net. This will increase the tax-to-GDP ratio and strengthen the revenue base.

Additionally, tax waiver opportunities should be rationalised. Revenue targets should also be realistic and evidence-based. It's not just about expanding the tax net but also restoring taxpayers' confidence. They need to be assured that tax money is being properly utilised and that quality in healthcare, education, and other government services is improving in return. If fairness, transparency, and accountability in the tax system are ensured, people's interest in paying taxes will also increase.

Recently, the salaries and allowances of government employees have been significantly increased. Questions have arisen about the source of its funding.

Mohammad Abu Eusuf: A new pay scale is being implemented 11 years after the 2015 national pay structure. During this time, inflation has increased, so salary adjustments have become necessary to maintain government employees' purchasing power. I consider the initiative to implement this pay scale in phases a strategic move, as implementing it all at once would create financial pressure on the government. The budget speech has also made provisions for funding this. This pay scale was overdue for government officials and staff. However, to meet this expenditure, the government must not rely on bank loans. Instead, revenue collection needs to increase.

In the future, instead of repeatedly forming pay commissions, salary adjustments should be made annually based on inflation. Particularly, the entry-level salaries of new government employees should also be adjusted based on inflation. If an effective system is established, regular salary adjustments are possible. This will eliminate the need for such significant increases in allowances in one go. The economic burden will not fall all at once.

Thank you.

Mohammad Abu Eusuf: Thank you, too

Former air chief Sheikh Abdul Hannan arrested in Qatar
item.description:
Former Chief of Air Staff Air Chief Marshal (retd) Sheikh Abdul Hannan, who is accused in a corruption case, has been arrested in Qatar.

Local police arrested him on 15 October. Interpol, the international police organisation, informed the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) of the arrest via an email.

An ACC official confirmed the information on Sunday. ACC Secretary Md Saidur Rahman Khan will brief the media on the matter in detail at a press conference this afternoon.

On 11 November last year, a court ordered the seizure of two flats owned by Sheikh Abdul Hannan, who is an accused in a corruption case, and the freezing of 10 of his bank accounts.

The ACC launched an inquiry into Sheikh Abdul Hannan in February 2025. In July that year, the commission filed a case against him over allegations of acquiring assets beyond his known sources of income.

Sheikh Abdul Hannan received his commission in the Bangladesh Air Force in 1984. He took office as the country’s 16th chief of air staff on 12 June 2021 and retired on 11 June 2024.

item.title: Drugs sold through websites, secret Telegram groups; two private universities targeted
item.description:
The Department of Narcotics Control (DNC) says it has uncovered an online drug-selling network operating around two private universities in the capital’s Bashundhara Residential Area. According to the agency, the network operates a website and a secret Telegram group where “kush” and synthetic cannabis are readily available.

According to DNC sources, a network has emerged that sells drugs online. Most of its members are university students. They distribute visiting cards to students who use drugs, approaching them as they move around campuses. The cards contain QR codes that direct interested people to a website. From there, they are invited to join a secret Telegram group.

Mohammad Mehedi Hasan, deputy director of the DNC’s Dhaka Divisional Intelligence Office, told Prothom Alo that drug dealers were increasingly using technology to devise new ways to sell drugs. Intelligence teams identify such activities through cyber patrolling and subsequently conduct raids, he said.

He added that the raid yielded high-potency synthetic cannabis, kush seeds and various items of drug-processing equipment. A student was arrested during the operation.

DNC sources said the agency was monitoring drug dealers’ activities both on the ground and online. Efforts were underway to identify those conducting drug businesses under the cover of technology and bring them to justice, they added.

‘250 students in Telegram group’

On Friday, a DNC team led by Assistant Director Mostak Ahmed raided a flat in the capital’s Bhatara area and arrested a young man, Saim Islam, 19, with 300 grams of cannabis.

During questioning, Saim told DNC officials that he was a student at a private university. He had created a website two months earlier to sell drugs online. He subsequently formed a secret Telegram group for people who expressed interest through the website. Around 250 students from two private universities who use drugs were members of the group, he said.

Citing Saim’s interrogation, officials said he had spent two months experimenting with different methods before beginning to sell “kush” and synthetic cannabis two weeks ago.

A student at a private university, who spoke to Prothom Alo on condition of anonymity, said several drug-dealing networks were active around private universities in the Bashundhara Residential Area. There were several drug hotspots, the student said, adding that drugs were increasingly being delivered to people’s homes after they placed orders online.

Following Saim’s arrest, DNC Inspector Mohammad Khorshed Alam filed a case with Bhatara police station.

According to the first information report (FIR), a DNC team conducted a raid in the area based on a tip-off. The team searched a flat and recovered 300 grams of cannabis wrapped in white polythene. A used mobile phone was also seized.

The FIR states that Saim, who was arrested in the case, is from Bakerganj in Barishal. He lived in a flat in the Lichubagan area of Joar Sahara, Bhatara.

item.title: Please don’t tie our hands, you’ll have to come to us again: Matiur Rahman Chowdhury
item.description:
Matiur Rahman Chowdhury, president of the Newspaper Owners’ Association of Bangladesh (NOAB) and editor-in-chief of Manabzamin, said that the incumbent government wants to enact laws to curb criticism, but those very laws end up being used against the government itself when it loses power.
Addressing the government, Matiur Rahman Chowdhury said, “Please don’t tie our hands again. If you tie our hands, it will be to your own detriment. I won’t be able to write in your favour anymore. One day, you will have to come back to us again.”
He made these remarks on Sunday morning at a roundtable discussion on the proposed Cyber Security (Amendment) Act, held at the office of Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) in Dhanmondi, Dhaka.
A total of 19 organisations, including TIB, BRAC, BLAST, and the Bangladesh Mahila Parishad, organised the meeting.
Matiur Rahman Chowdhury said that power is not permanent anywhere in the world. He remarked that laws should therefore be drafted with the future in mind.
The editor of Manabzamin said that laws are necessary to combat cybercrime. However, he stressed that criticism of the government must be distinguished from cyber crime. “There will inevitably be criticism of the government; that is perfectly normal in a democratic society. If these two are not treated separately, the danger will remain,” he said.
The NOAB president also questioned a provision in the proposed Cyber Security Act that would allow newspapers or online news outlets to be shut down over an offence committed by an individual. Expressing concern about how the law might be enforced, he warned of the risk of political interference. He said that a phone call from a ruling party leader at the local level could potentially lead to someone’s arrest.
Matiur Rahman Chowdhury also questioned the definition of “misinformation” in the proposed law. In his view, a news report could be labelled as misinformation or accused of being published with the intention of defaming someone simply because that person disliked its contents. He said there must be a clear answer to the question of who would determine whether information was deliberately false.
Matiur Rahman Chowdhury opposed granting mobile courts the authority to try journalists. He said, “You are giving the power to try journalists to the same mobile courts that are used to catch people who manufacture adulterated medicines! How can such a thing even be contemplated in a democratic society?”
Matiur Rahman Chowdhury called for discussions on the proposed law to be held across districts and for opinions to be sought from people from all walks of life. He also urged the authorities to ensure that the committee responsible for drafting the law included representatives from diverse social and professional backgrounds.
The meeting was moderated by Iftekharuzzaman, executive director of Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB). Participants included Mohammad Shahidul Islam, president of the Dhaka Journalists union (DJU); Shafiqul Alam, editor of Daily Wada; Sharifuzzaman Pintu, convener of the Online Editors Forum; and Fouzia Afroz, Bangladesh head of the Tech Global Institute, among others.

item.title: Prime accused Amini used different SIM cards, phones to evade arrest
item.description:
Police have arrested Fazlul Haque Amini, 45, the prime accused in the murder of Wahiduzzaman Shamim, 38, who was beaten to death in Debhata of Satkhira.

He was arrested at around 11:00 pm on Saturday at a relative’s house in Faridpur village under Kaliganj upazila of Satkhira. Police said they were trying to identify and arrest others involved in the incident.

A joint operation involving members of the Debhata Circle, Kaliganj police station, Debhata police station and Special Response Battalion (SRB)-6 led to Amini’s arrest. Shamim was beaten to death in Debhata last Tuesday over allegations that he had hurt religious sentiments. He was a resident of Subarnabad village in Debhata.

Debhata police station officer-in-charge (OC) HM Shaheen told Prothom Alo on Sunday morning that Amini had been arrested on a tipoff and with the help technology. He was not carrying his own mobile phone at the time of his arrest. Instead, he had been using different SIM cards and phones.

Amini used one of those SIM cards to speak to someone while identifying himself. Investigators traced him through that communication. No significant information has yet emerged from his initial questioning. He will be produced before a court today, and police will seek seven days’ remand.

Man beaten to death in Satkhira: Main accused Ameni arrested

Shamim’s elder brother, Abdul Jalil, filed the murder case on Thursday night. Amini was named as the prime accused, along with 10 other people identified by name and another 200 to 250 unidentified individuals.

Police arrested the fifth and sixth accused named in the case, Moktar Hossain Khan, 53, and Asadul Islam Molla, 46, early on Friday and sent them to jail.

The OC said several people had been identified by analysing CCTV footage and mobile phone data.

Shamim’s younger brother, Tausif Rahman, said, “We feel somewhat relieved by the news of the prime accused’s arrest. Now we have only one demand: that the state ensure a fair trial for the injustice done to my brother. Those involved in this incident should receive the maximum punishment under the existing law and judicial process. The government should also stand by my brother’s two orphaned children, keeping their future in mind.”

Calling for the arrest of the other accused, Tausif said that if the second and third accused, Kamrul Gazi and Sadikul, were arrested, more information might emerge about who was involved and who played the leading roles in the incident.

He claimed that Kamrul Gazi was the president of Puliya Union Ward no. 8 Jamaat-e-Islami unit. However, the family was unsure of Sadikul’s political identity.

Debhata upazila Jamaat secretary Imdadul Haque told Prothom Alo that the murder of Shamim by beating him to death could not be justified under any circumstances. Condemning the incident, he said Jamaat did not support this kind of violence.

Asked about Kamrul Gazi, the Ward no. 8 Jamaat unit president, being named in the case, Imdadul Haque said they believed he had been implicated as part of a conspiracy.

He claimed that Kamrul Gazi was not at the scene and that his name had been included with malicious intent. Imdadul Haque also alleged that the incident had been politically motivated.

Man beaten to death in Satkhira after Facebook Live draws a crowd

Shamim’s family said he had been suffering from mental health issues for a long time. On Monday, an audio recording of an argument between him and his wife circulated on social media. After allegations emerged that the recording contained derogatory remarks about religion, an attempt was made to attack his house, and he was beaten at a local market.

Shamim’s family said he later ingested poison. While he was receiving treatment at the chamber of local village physician Md Sabur, more than 100 people gathered there the following day, dragged him outside and beat him. Police rescued him from there and took him to Debhata Upazila Health Complex.

Debhata Upazila Health Complex health and family planning officer Md Saiful Islam said that after Shamim was admitted to hospital, more than 100 people entered the ward and beat him again. Ansar members, security personnel and hospital staff failed to stop them. Police later rescued him and were taking him to Satkhira Medical College Hospital when he died on the way.

Several cameras at the hospital were disconnected, making it impossible to view all the footage. Police have not yet requested the footage, but the hospital authorities are trying to preserve it.

item.title: Police file case against 23, including resort owner; manager arrested
item.description:
Police have filed a case against 23 people over a fire at Tuptup Resort in Patuartek, Ukhiya, Cox’s Bazar. The resort’s owner, Md Tanvir, has been named as the prime accused. The case was filed late Saturday night by Ashis Sutradhar, a sub-inspector of Ukhiya Police Station.

Ukhiya Police Station Officer-in-Charge Atikur Rahman Majumder confirmed the case on Sunday morning. He said four people had been named in the case, including resort owner Md Tanvir and Newaz Morshed. The remaining accused are unidentified.

Resort manager Zahidul Islam, also known as Sumon, was detained at the scene on Saturday afternoon and has since been shown arrested in the case.

10 tourists killed in fire at Inani resort flagged as risky in June: Fire Service

Police have yet to determine how the fire started. Cox’s Bazar Superintendent of Police ANM Sajedur Rahman said on Sunday morning that no definitive statement could be made about the cause until the investigation was complete. The investigation would establish how the fire began, he said.

According to local residents, the fire broke out at the resort, which is located beside the Marine Drive road, at around 7:30 am on Saturday. Fire service personnel arrived after receiving the alert. Local residents then joined the efforts to contain the blaze and rescue people, with assistance from police.

Mohammad Taufiqul Islam Bhuiyan, deputy director of the Fire Service and Civil Defence in Chattogram division, said Cox’s Bazar Fire Service received the report of the fire at 7:23 am. Firefighters reached the scene at around 8:00 am, and the blaze was brought under control at 8:15 am.

Of the 10 people killed in the fire, four died in two toilets on the resort’s second floor, he said.

Taufiqul Islam Bhuiyan said strong sea winds caused the fire to spread rapidly through the wooden resort. Such establishments should have portable fire extinguishers, fire alarms, hosepipes and a fire safety plan. But, the resort had none of these facilities. It also lacked a fire safety licence.

Cox’s Bazar resort fire: 6 family members die, man survives by jumping from first floor

The resort had been built only seven to eight months earlier. There was also a dispute over ownership of the land, he said.

Subaktagin Mahmud Sohel, resident medical officer at Cox’s Bazar Sadar Hospital, said the identities of six of the 10 victims had been provisionally established. However, authorities had not yet confirmed which body belonged to which victim.

The deceased include Israt Jahan, 30, and Milita Mehezabin, 23, from Dhaka’s Banasree; Laila Jahan, 27, and Nafista Mim, 27, from Khilgaon; Fariha Kabir, 33, from Chuadanga; and five-year-old Faizan Ahmed.

The identities of the other four victims remain unknown. They include two women, one child and one man.

item.title: Freedom fighter and artist Saeeda Kamal dies at 74
item.description:
Freedom fighter and Artist Saeeda Kamal has passed away. She died at around 7:30 am on Sunday (18 October), at a private hospital in Dhaka . She was 74 years old.

Saeeda Kamal was the daughter of renowned poet Sufia Kamal and the younger sister of Sultana Kamal, a former caretaker government adviser and chairperson of the human rights platform Amrai Pari. Sultana Kamal confirmed the news of her passing.

According to family sources, Saeeda Kamal had been suffering from multiple health complications for a long time. She had recently been admitted to the hospital's Intensive Care Unit (ICU), where she breathed her last.

She leaves behind an only daughter who lives abroad.

Her family added that Saeeda Kamal made notable contributions to the country's art scene through her creative works. After studying fine arts at the University of Dhaka, she trained in design at Kala Bhavana in Santiniketan.

Her artworks were showcased in numerous solo and joint exhibitions both at home and abroad.

During the 1971 Liberation War, Saeeda Kamal served alongside her elder sister Sultana Kamal at the frontline Bangladesh Field Hospital, treating wounded freedom fighters.

For her valiant service, she was awarded the Commander-in-Chief’s Special Commendation (CinC’s Special Commendation).

item.title: Question leak controversy: 5,386 pass repeat recruitment test
item.description:
The results of the preliminary recruitment examination for the post of assistant upazila youth development officer at the Department of Youth Development have been published, with 5,386 candidates passing. The list of successful candidates has been published in a notice on the department’s website.

The recruitment examination for 242 vacant posts of assistant upazila youth development officer under the Department of Youth Development’s revenue budget was scheduled for 10 October. More than 300,000 candidates had applied for the 242 posts. However, the question paper was circulated on social media before the examination began.

Written contracts for leaked job exam questions at Tk 1 million

As the leaked questions were found to match the original paper, the examination was suspended just two minutes after it started. Many candidates who had travelled from distant areas were angered by the decision and blocked roads and staged protests at various locations in the capital that day.

A new date was announced for the cancelled examination for the 11th-grade post following allegations that the question paper had been leaked. The preliminary screening test was held again on Friday, 16 October 2026. The results were published yesterday, Saturday. The date, time and venue of the written examination for successful candidates will be announced later.

Youth Development Department to hold exam despite question paper leak

Details of the next stage will be communicated through the Department of Youth Development’s website and text messages sent via Teletalk. An office order on the matter also states that a candidate’s application or result will be cancelled if they engage in irregularities or use unfair means at any stage of the recruitment process.

A five-member committee, headed by Mohammad Mahfuzul Alam Khan, an additional secretary at the Ministry of Youth and Sports, was formed to investigate the question leak. The committee was initially asked to submit its report within three working days, but the deadline was later extended.

The Special Response Battalion (SRB) has arrested seven people in a case filed over the question leak. They were sent to jail by court order on Saturday.

item.title: SSC form fill-up dates announced for 2027; six key instructions for candidates
item.description:
The schedule for online form fill-up and fee payment for the 2027 Secondary School Certificate (SSC) examinations has been announced. The process will begin on 16 November, and candidates will be able to complete their forms online without a late fee until 23 November. The information was announced in a notice issued by the Dhaka Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education.

The board has issued specific instructions for candidates seeking GPA improvement and those previously expelled from examinations. Students who passed all subjects in the 2026 SSC examinations but obtained a GPA below 5.00 will be eligible to sit for the 2027 examinations to improve their GPA, provided their registration remains valid. They must take examinations in all subjects under the full 2026 syllabus.

The board’s instructions cover several important issues relating to form fill-up for the 2027 SSC examinations. Six key areas are outlined below.

1.       GPA improvement

Candidates who took examinations in all subjects in 2026 and passed but obtained a GPA below 5.00 may sit for the 2027 examinations to improve their GPA, provided their registration remains valid. They must take examinations in all subjects under the full 2026 syllabus.

If their GPA improves in the 2027 examinations, the new result will be accepted. Otherwise, their previous GPA will remain unchanged. Candidates seeking GPA improvement must submit printed, attested photocopies of their previous examination admit cards and academic transcripts along with their forms.

2.       Candidates previously expelled

Candidates whose period of punishment for expulsion has ended may sit for the 2027 SSC examinations as irregular candidates, provided their registration remains valid. They must take examinations in all subjects.

3.       Benefits of the fourth subject

Candidates registered in the 2023–24 and 2024–25 academic years who did not sit for the 2025 or 2026 examinations may sit for the 2027 examinations as irregular candidates, taking all subjects, including the fourth subject.

Candidates registered in those two academic years who took all subjects in the 2025 or 2026 SSC examinations, passed the fourth subject but failed one to four other subjects, will be eligible for the benefit of the fourth subject if they pass the subject or subjects they previously failed in the 2027 examinations.

4.       Syllabus and assessment

a.       Irregular candidates and those seeking GPA improvement will sit for examinations based on question papers prepared in accordance with the syllabuses used for the 2025 and 2026 SSC examinations.

b.       Regular candidates will sit for examinations based on question papers prepared in accordance with the syllabus for the 2027 SSC examinations.

c.       For students of all academic years, marks obtained through continuous assessment in Physical Education, Health Science and Sports, and Career Education must be submitted by educational institutions to the relevant examination centres in accordance with National Curriculum and Textbook Board (NCTB) guidelines. The centres must upload these marks to the board’s website alongside practical examination marks. The original handwritten mark sheets for continuous assessment in practical subjects must also be submitted in person to the board’s Secondary Examination Branch.

5.       Selection examinations

Participation in selection examinations is compulsory for all students except those seeking GPA improvement and those who have already sat for an SSC examination but failed.

6.       Rules for irregular candidates

a.       Students registered in the 2023–24 and 2024–25 academic years who did not sit for the 2025 or 2026 SSC examinations may participate in the 2027 examinations as irregular candidates through their respective educational institutions. They cannot be treated as regular candidates under any circumstances.

b.       Candidates who took all subjects in the 2026 SSC examinations but failed one to four subjects, excluding the fourth subject, may sit for the 2027 examinations in the subject or subjects they failed, provided their registration remains valid. They may also choose to sit for all subjects.

c.       Candidates who failed one to three subjects, excluding the fourth subject, in the 2025 SSC examinations and either did not sit for the 2026 examinations or sat for them but failed one or more subjects again may sit for the 2027 examinations as irregular candidates, provided their registration remains valid. They may take the subjects they previously failed or sit for all subjects. Candidates opting to take only the subjects they failed will not be allowed to sit for the fourth subject.

d.       Students registered in the 2022–23 academic year whose registration has expired but who still have one failed subject, excluding the fourth subject, may be granted a special one-year extension of their registration. They may then sit for the failed subject in the 2027 SSC examinations as irregular candidates.

Candidates covered by clauses b to d will retain the grade points earned in subjects they previously passed. Their GPA will be calculated by adding the grade points earned in the subjects they take in 2027 to the retained grade points for subjects they passed earlier.

Before form fill-up begins, the head of the educational institution of a candidate covered by clause d must submit the original registration card to the board’s Office of the School Inspector and collect the renewed registration card.
